sens: Family of temple workers who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H5300.detail: 1. Nephischsim is the name of a family of temple workers (its members were called the sons of Nephischsim). This family was part of the exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel after the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem. They are found in the list of the inhabitants of Jerusalem who contributed to the restoration of the Lord's worship.
H5300.origine: The name Nephischsim literally means "those refreshed by spices" or expresses the idea of being restored and revitalized. Like many family names in the Bible, this name comes from an eponymous ancestor named Nephus. It is a family among the temple servants, a category of people assigned to work in the service of the sanctuary.
H5300.emploi: Nephischsim appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 7:52. The text lists the names of the families who returned from Babylonian captivity. These return lists (also found in Ezra 2) show how the Jewish people were reconstituted after the exile. The descendants of the temple servants, like those of Nephischsim, resumed their service in the restored temple.
H5300.portee: This passage reminds us that God did not abandon His people in exile and that even the temple servants were able to return to restore worship. It is evidence of God's faithfulness to Israel and His desire to rebuild His sanctuary.

sens: To expel air through the mouth or nose forcefully
To animate or give life by breathing in
To ignite or rekindle a fire by blowing on it
To act with power and destruction, like divine wind or fire
H5301.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical and concrete: to blow is to expel air forcefully. This is what a worker does when he blows on the coal to stoke the fire (Isaiah 54:16), or the wind that strikes violently.

2. The word also refers to the act of giving life by breathing in the vital breath. When the Lord God "blew" into the nostrils of the man formed from dust, He gave him life (Genesis 2:7) — it is the image of the Creator animating His creature by His breath.

3. To blow can also mean to annihilate or destroy: the Lord "blows" on the harvest of Haggai, making it barren and useless (Haggai 1:9), like a devastating wind or a consuming fire.

4. Finally, the word evokes the powerful and fearsome divine action: the Lord "blows" against Jerusalem with the fire of His fury to consume it (Ezekiel 22:21). It is the expression of divine judgment, earthly and irresistible.
H5301.origine: The Hebrew word naḥphach comes from a root that paints the image of breath and wind. It belongs to the family of words related to breath: it is connected to the word "neshama" (the soul, the vital breath). The word primarily expresses a physical act—breathing, blowing—before becoming an image of creative or destructive power. In Hebrew thought, breath is always alive: God's breath creates, man's breath lives, and breath can annihilate like the violence of the wind.
H5301.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books and among the prophets. Its most famous usage is in Genesis 2:7, where God breathes life into man: it is the foundational image of the link between the divine and the human. Among the prophets, particularly Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, "to blow" describes the action of divine judgment: God blows against His enemies or upon His creation to transform or destroy it. In Haggai 1:9, it also expresses cancellation, the effect of nothingness: what should prosper is rendered vain. The word never denotes a mere whisper, but a powerful, conscious, effective action.
H5301.portee: This word reveals to the believer that life comes from God and depends on His breath: it is an invitation to recognize the absolute sovereignty of the Creator over our existence. It also shows that God is not distant or indifferent, but that He acts in history with power—either to vivify or to judge. For the reader, "to blow" becomes a key to understanding divine action: it is alive, voluntary, and it transforms everything it touches.

sens: Location in the region of Moab, in Transjordan
H5302.detail: Nophach is a city in Moab, a region east of the Jordan. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 21:30, in the account of the Israelites' victory over Sihon, king of the Amorites. The text lists the cities destroyed during this conquest: "From Heshbon to Dibon all is destroyed; We have extended our ravages to Nophach, To Medeba." It represents the northern limit of the devastated area in this region.
H5302.origine: The name Nophach comes from the Hebrew נֹפַח (no.phach), which evokes the image of a "blast" or "explosion" (related to breath or destructive breath). It is another name for Kenath (קְנָת), a city that the Manassites settled after the conquest (Numbers 32:42). The double name likely reflects different local designations or distinct historical periods.
H5302.emploi: Nophach appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 21:30. It is included in the victory poem sung by the Israelites after their triumph over Sihon and his army. It is mentioned alongside Heshbon, Dibon, and Medeba, all major cities in the Moabite region. Its inclusion in this poetic text indicates its strategic importance in the geography of the conquered territories east of the Jordan.

sens: mythical giants of ancient times
beings of great size and superhuman strength
H5303.detail: 1. The Nephilim are extraordinary creatures mentioned at the beginnings of biblical humanity. Genesis 6:4 presents them as beings born from the union of the sons of God and the daughters of men — a union against nature that produced creatures of exceptional power and stature. 2. During the exploration of Canaan, the Israelite spies see Nephilim and are terrified: "We saw the Nephilim there" (Numbers 13:33). They represent a terrifying opposition to God's plan for Israel, obstacles that seem humanly insurmountable.
H5303.origine: The word "Nephilim" comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the fall or abatement. The name suggests beings that are fallen or brought low — either because they have fallen from heaven or because they bring down (overcome) what stands before them. This term designates a reality that the Bible presents as exceptional and anomalous in the history of salvation.
H5303.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible. The first occurrence, in Genesis 6:4, places them in a remote time, before the flood, as a result of illegitimate unions. The second, in Numbers 13:33, places them in Canaan after the flood: the spies will tell the Israelites that the inhabitants of the land are Nephilim (or at least related to them), which amplifies their fear and disbelief. This presence in two distinct contexts shows that the Bible considers the Nephilim as supernatural adversaries embodying rebellion against the divine order.
H5303.portee: The Nephilim remind us that faith in God does not rest on human strength or physical appearance. Their mention in Numbers invites the reader to ask: will the Israelites fear the giants more than God? The text's answer is implicit: only trust in the word and power of the Lord allows one to overcome obstacles that seem insurmountable.

sens: Family of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H5304.detail: 1. The Nephusim form a family of servants attached to the temple, mentioned in the list of exiles who returned from Babylon. The name appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:50, where they are listed among the descendants of the servants of Solomon who participated in the return with Zerubbabel after the captivity.
H5304.origine: The name Nephusim (נְפִישְׁסִים in Hebrew) literally means "scattered spices." It likely comes from a root that evokes what is sown or dispersed. The term is similar to other names of families of temple servants, characteristic of the genealogical lists of the return from exile.
H5304.emploi: Nephusim appears only once in the provided usages, in Ezra 2:50. It is a mention in the midst of a long enumeration of families who left Babylon to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem after 586 B.C. These genealogical lists testify to the historical reality of the return from exile and allowed for the verification of the identity of the families returning to their land.

sens: Son of Ishmael
Arab tribe of the desert
Warrior people in conflict with Israel
H5305.detail:
1. Naphisch is the second-to-last son of Ishmael, listed among the twelve sons from whom the Arab peoples descend (Genesis 25:15). He appears in the official genealogy of Ishmael, alongside his brothers Nebajoth, Kedar, Tema, and others.
2. Naphisch also designates the Arab tribe that bears his name, established in the desert like the other descendants of Ishmael. This tribe forms a distinct community among the peoples of Arabia.
3. In the history of Israel, the Naphischites appear as military adversaries: the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh fought against them, as well as against the Hagarites and Nodab (1 Chronicles 5:19), showing that this Arab tribe was a military power in the desert with which the Israelites had to contend.
H5305.origine: The name means "refreshment" or "relief" in Hebrew. Naphisch is the personal name of a son of Ishmael, from whom the tribe that bears his name descends. Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar, is the ancestor of the Arab peoples, and Naphisch is one of his twelve founding sons.
H5305.emploi: Naphisch appears three times in the Bible. First in the genealogy of Genesis 25:15, where he is listed among the twelve sons of Ishmael. Then in 1 Chronicles 1:31, where the same genealogy is repeated as an official record of the descendants of Ishmael. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 5:19, where the transjordanian tribes of Israel engage in battle against the Naphischites and other desert peoples, showing that this tribe was a political and military player in the history of the ancient Near East.

sens: Red or glowing precious stone
Gem of the high priest's breastplate
Luxury gem from the trade of Tyre
H5306.detail:
1. The escarboucle is a precious stone of red or glowing color — possibly a ruby, a garnet (pyrope), a red tourmaline, or another brilliant gem. It is listed among the precious stones in the Bible, always alongside other remarkable jewels.
2. It held a place of honor in the breastplate of the high priest, the garment that expressed his sacred function and his connection with the twelve tribes of Israel. This stone was set in the second row, signifying its exceptional value and ritual role (Exodus 28:18).
3. The escarboucle was among the precious goods that Syria (Aram) traded with Tyre, alongside purple, coral, and fine embroidery (Ezekiel 27:16). It symbolized the wealth and prestige of ancient Eastern trade.
H5306.origine: The Hebrew word "nopèkh" designates a brilliant and colorful stone; its root may evoke brightness or brilliance. The exact identity of the stone remains debated by scholars — it could be a ruby, a red garnet, or another gem from the ancient Near East. What is biblically important is that it is a very precious stone, symbolizing wealth and brilliance.
H5306.emploi: The word appears four times in the Bible, always to denote a stone of great value. Twice, it is found in the breastplate of the high priest (Exodus 28:18 and 39:11), integrated into the ritual garment that embodied the priest's spiritual responsibility toward Israel. Two other times (Ezekiel 27:16 and 28:13), it appears in enumerations of precious wealth: first as a luxurious trade item between Tyre and Syria, then in the poetic description of the original splendor of the king of Tyre in Eden. In all cases, the escarboucle symbolizes excellence, prestige, and incomparable beauty.
H5306.portee: The escarboucle reminds us that beauty and value mark the presence of God — in the priest's garment that represents Him, and in the creation of Eden that reflected His glory. It invites us to contemplate how God's works are perfect and splendid, and how sacred service demands the best and most beautiful.

sens: To descend from high to low, to lose footing, to physically fall
To die in battle, to be killed in war
To prostrate oneself, to kneel respectfully before someone
To succumb, to be defeated, to be delivered to an enemy
To fail, to not succeed, to miss one's goal
To happen, to occur, to result as a consequence
H5307G.detail:
1. To fall means to descend involuntarily: someone or something loses balance and tumbles down. The Lord caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam (Genesis 2:21), meaning that sleep overwhelmed him, engulfed him like a fall. The wall of Babylon falls (Jeremiah 51:44), it collapses, crumbles.
2. To fall in battle means to be killed, to perish with arms in hand. Men who fall in combat lose their lives (1 Samuel 31:8 shows corpses found after the battle).
3. To fall face down means to prostrate oneself: Joab "falls" face down to honor the king (2 Samuel 14:22). It is a gesture of submission and respect, where the body voluntarily collapses before an authority.
4. To fall into someone's hand means to be defeated, delivered to him. When a city "falls," it is conquered, it becomes prey to the enemy.
5. To fall short means to fail, to not reach one's goal. Job says he is not "inferior" to others, that he does not fall short (Job 12:3): he does not fall short in wisdom.
6. To fall can also mean to happen, to occur, to be the result. The things that happen to you "fall" upon you; it is what naturally ensues.
H5307G.origine: The Hebrew verb נָפַל (naphàl) evokes the idea of losing grip, letting go, no longer holding. Its basic image is that of a fall: something that was standing or suspended suddenly crashes down. This root is found in several Semitic languages with the same meaning. The different forms of the verb nuance this meaning: the simple form (Qal) describes the fall itself, while the causative form (Hiphil) means "to make fall," that is, to overturn, to knock down, to bring someone down.
H5307G.emploi: To fall is one of the most frequent verbs in the Hebrew Bible: 262 occurrences. It appears as early as Genesis (sleep falls on Adam, Abraham falls face down before God) and throughout historical narratives. In the Law (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), it describes things that fall and render them unclean (Leviticus 11:32-38). In the books of Samuel, to fall often denotes death in battle or prostration. In Proverbs and Jeremiah, to fall takes on a figurative sense: one "falls" into a trap, one "falls" into ruin. The word applies to both the physical (a man collapsing) and the spiritual (a city crumbling) and behavior (to prostrate oneself, to accept defeat). Its meaning varies according to context: sometimes it is involuntary and tragic, sometimes it is a voluntary act of reverence.
H5307G.portee: To fall reveals human fragility before God and the world. When a man prostrates himself by falling, he acknowledges a higher power and accepts the established order. When a wall falls, it shows that no barrier withstands divine will. This verb reminds us that our plans can collapse, that our enemies can defeat us, but also that respectful submission is a form of wisdom. It is a word that anchors faith in the concrete reality of our falls and our surrender.

sens: To fall physically, to be overturned or struck down
To die violently, to be killed in battle
To prostrate oneself, to kneel before someone
To pass to someone, to surrender, to join
To be distributed, to fall by lot
To occur, to happen, to take place
H5307H.detail:
1. To fall or be overturned from a standing position: this is to lose balance and fall, or to be thrown to the ground. Exodus 21:27 speaks of making a slave's tooth "fall out."
2. To fall also means to die violently, to be killed in war or battle. This is a death that occurs by force, not by old age.
3. To prostrate oneself before someone as a sign of respect or submission: to fall face down to honor a king or a god.
4. To pass to someone, to surrender to them, particularly in a military sense: to abandon a camp to join the enemy or a rival leader. Jeremiah 37:13 and 38:19 speak of those who "pass" to the Chaldeans, meaning they join or submit to them.
5. To be distributed or allocated by lot, often by the decision of a leader. Proverbs 1:14 speaks of having one's "share" with others in a common booty.
6. To occur, to happen, to take place: an event or state that befalls someone, such as a calamity or punishment.
H5307H.origine: The Hebrew verb נָפַל (naphal) primarily evokes the physical image of falling, collapsing. It comes from a very ancient root that has produced many compounds and derived names in Hebrew. Its basic meaning easily projects onto military (to be defeated, to fall in battle), religious (to prostrate), or political (to pass to an ally or enemy) domains. It is a very frequent word in the Old Testament, serving to express both the concrete and figurative realities of falling, defeat, fate, or submission.
H5307H.emploi: The verb נָפַל appears 14 times in the provided references, covering several domains. In the most concrete sense, it denotes a physical action: to make a tooth fall (Exodus 21:27). In military and political contexts, it expresses the passage of a person to an opposing camp: soldiers or civilians who "surrender" to the Chaldeans, or who "join" a leader like David (1 Chronicles 12:20). It also means distribution, allocation by lot (Proverbs 1:14). Finally, the word can describe violent death or the arrival of an event. Its usage varies according to context: "to fall" in the literal sense, "to surrender" or "to pass" in a war context, "to fall by lot" or "to have a share" in a distribution context.
H5307H.portee: This word reminds us that human life is fragile and subject to forces beyond it — death, defeat, falling. But it also speaks of voluntary submission before God and His power to distribute fates. For the believer, to fall can mean to stumble into sin, but also to prostrate oneself before the Lord in acknowledgment, or to surrender to Him by accepting His authority. It is a word that traverses both God's judgment and the necessity of humility.

sens: To fall, to collapse, to be struck down
To attack, to descend upon someone
To fail, to not succeed
To assign or share by lot
H5307I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to fall or collapse, like a body losing balance or a structure collapsing. The image also evokes violent falling in battle or death in war.
2. In a military or hostile context, the word denotes a sudden attack: to descend upon the enemy, to assail. It is the idea of falling *upon* someone with violence.
3. Figuratively, the word expresses failure or insufficiency: to fail to accomplish something, to not succeed. For example, "he did not receive an inheritance" (Judges 18:1) means he did not obtain his share.
4. The most frequent meaning in our biblical usages is legal and religious: *to draw lots*, that is, to assign something by a process of chance or divination. "They drew lots for their duties" (1 Chronicles 25:8): lots are cast to decide who will do what. This drawing is seen as a divine decision, not a human one.
H5307I.origine: The Hebrew verb נָפַל (naphal) is a simple verb whose root evokes the physical idea of falling or being struck down. In Hebrew, most meanings derive from this primary image: what falls is distributed, what falls upon someone strikes them, what falls fails to remain standing. Drawing lots operates by an analogous logic: lots are allowed to fall, and the one that falls determines the outcome. The word also appears with complements that specify: "to fall *into* the hands of," "to fall *before*" (to prostrate), "to fall *upon*" (to attack).
H5307I.emploi: The verb נָפַל appears 22 times in the provided usages, covering the entire Old Testament. The dominant meaning is drawing lots or assigning by lot: this is the context of 1 Chronicles 25:8, Nehemiah 10:34, Esther 3:7 and 9:24, Isaiah 34:17, Ezekiel 45:1 and 47:14-22. In these passages, lots are drawn to distribute tasks (priestly functions), designate leaders, determine victims (Esther), or share the promised lands. The second important meaning is allocation or inheritance: "he did not receive an inheritance" (Judges 18:1) or "this land will become your inheritance" (Numbers 34:2: the verb means "to fall as possession"). These usages show that drawing lots was a common practice in Israel for religious and administrative matters, legitimized as an expression of divine will.
H5307I.portee: This word reminds believers that important decisions are not left to chance: when drawing lots in the Bible, one expects God to speak through this means. The Lord controls even the dice (Proverbs 16:33). Drawing lots was also a way to set aside human ambitions and recognize God's authority. Today, this word invites Christians to meditate on divine providence: even in what seems accidental, God directs events according to His wisdom.

sens: To tilt downward, to lose balance
To be killed, to perish in battle or by violent death
To prostrate oneself, to throw oneself to the ground in a sign of respect or submission
To fall upon someone, to attack or seize them
To fail, to not succeed, to disappear
H5307J.detail:
1. To fall means to lose balance and tilt downward: a descending physical movement. This is the most concrete meaning of the word, that of a body collapsing under itself or under a shock.

2. To fall in battle means to be killed, to perish by violent death: it is to fall and not rise again. In 1 Samuel 31:1, the men of Israel "fell dead on the mountain of Gilboa," and in Joshua 8:25, "twelve thousand people were killed" — the Hebrew word expresses both the fall and the death.

3. To prostrate oneself is to voluntarily throw oneself to the ground, face down, in a sign of respect, worship, or submission before someone greater. In Genesis 44:14, Judah and his brothers "prostrated themselves on the ground before Joseph": it is to fall intentionally, with reverence.

4. To fall upon someone means to come down against them, to attack or seize them with force. In Psalms 37:14, the wicked draw the bow "to make the unfortunate fall" — evil comes upon him, assailing him.

5. To fail or not succeed: the word also describes the collapse of a project, a hope, or a life. It is to not stand, to morally or spiritually collapse.
H5307J.origine: The Hebrew verb נָפַל (naphal) is a very ancient root that primarily denotes the simple movement of falling, that of an object or a person collapsing. The image is clear: to lose footing, to tilt downward. From this primary image arise all the meanings of the word — to die in battle is to fall; to prostrate oneself is to choose to fall before God; to fail is to see one's project collapse. The word has a causative form (to make fall, to overturn) which means to cause someone else to fall. This root is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible and remains simple: it depicts reality through a gesture that can be seen.
H5307J.emploi: The verb naphal is one of the most used in the Hebrew Bible: 92 occurrences according to the provided text. It is omnipresent in battle narratives (Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel, 2 Chronicles) where it means to be killed: "his young men will fall in the streets" (Jeremiah 50:30). It is also found in the laws (Leviticus, Deuteronomy) concerning land allotments or cases of death. It appears in the Psalms and the prophets to express misfortune, collapse, or ruin. The word slightly changes tone depending on the context: the tomb of a warrior signifies glorious or shameful death; to fall before God is to worship; to fall ill or die is to undergo divine judgment. This flexibility makes it a key word for understanding fate, battle, death, and worship in the Bible.
H5307J.portee: To understand "to fall" in the Bible is to grasp that physical and moral collapse is a biblical language for human vulnerability, defeat, and death. But it is also to recognize that to prostrate oneself, to fall before God in worship, is the foundational act of faith: voluntary surrender, trust, renouncing to stand alone. The word invites the believer to see in every fall — that of an army, that of a proud nation, that of a sinner — the judgment or call of God, and in prostration an act of wisdom and life.

sens: To physically fall, to lose footing
To collapse, to be struck down by violence or death
To prostrate oneself, to throw oneself to the ground in submission or worship
To rush against someone, to attack
To fail, to miss one's goal, to not keep promises
To become dark, to darken (referring to the face or gaze)
H5307K.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to fall to the ground, to tumble, to lose balance or vertical position. This is the base image from which all other meanings derive.
2. To fall in battle, to be killed, to succumb to violence — a definitive, irreversible fall, like that of a warrior struck dead.
3. To throw oneself to the ground voluntarily in a sign of respect, humility, or worship before someone more powerful — not an accidental fall, but a deliberate act of submission.
4. To rush at someone with force, to attack, to pounce on them — the image of the fall applied to the aggressor who leaps upon their prey.
5. To miss one's objective, to fail, to falter — in a figurative sense: promises that do not come to pass, commitments that collapse. In Genesis 4:5, Cain "fell" into anger, his self-control collapsed.
6. A gaze or face that becomes dark, that darkens under the weight of anger or sadness — as if physical features "fell" under the effect of emotion. In Jeremiah 3:12, God says that he will not cast a severe look: literally, he will not let (his gaze) fall with anger.
H5307K.origine: The verb נָפַל (naphal) comes from a root that describes the movement of descending, collapsing, or losing position. The word belongs to a rich family: נְפִילִים (nephilim) refers to giants, those who have "fallen" from heaven or of imposing stature. In Greek, this Hebrew verb is often translated as πίπτω (piptô, "to fall"). The base image — physical and concrete — naturally extends to the moral, emotional, and spiritual realm: to fall morally is to fail; to fall in face is to show anger or shame.
H5307K.emploi: The verb נָפַל appears about 150 times in the Old Testament, in historical narratives, psalms, and prophets. In Genesis 4:5, Cain "fell" meaning he was overtaken by anger — the verb here denotes an emotional state that suddenly and irresistibly seizes him. In Jeremiah 3:12, the prophet uses the verb in the sense of gaze or favor that turns away: God says he will not let his severe gaze fall, in other words, he will not turn his face away in anger. The context is one of repentance and forgiveness: even if Israel has sinned, God does not reject them. The word also plays on the idea of the face that "falls" when anger rises — a vivid and expressive phrase.
H5307K.portee: This richness of meaning reminds us that falling — whether physical or moral — is omnipresent in human life. But the word also reveals God's mercy: in Jeremiah 3:12, he promises that his anger will not "fall" upon the repentant. For the believer, understanding this range of meanings (fall, collapse, defeat, but also prostration before God) helps to grasp both our fragility and the possibility of throwing ourselves at God's mercy with confidence.

sens: Descend to the bottom, lose balance or support
Die in battle, be struck down
Prostrate oneself, bow before someone
Be defeated, fail, not come to fruition
Come to someone, befall as a share
H5307L.detail:
1. The primary and most concrete meaning: to fall physically, to lose footing. It is the movement from high to low, when one loses balance or is thrown to the ground — the basic image from which all other uses derive.

2. To fall in battle, to die on the battlefield. A warrior who "falls" is a warrior struck down. David says to Saul: "Your servant has killed the lion and the bear; this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them" (1 Samuel 17:32), showing that he has faced and overcome danger, while Goliath is the one who falls.

3. To prostrate oneself, to throw oneself at someone's feet to honor or plead with them. It is also a form of respect: to fall before someone is to acknowledge their superiority.

4. To fail, not come to fruition, "remain without effect." When it is said that a word "does not remain without effect," it means that it does not fall (it does not collapse), that it does not become void, that it reaches its goal. Joshua 21:45 affirms that all of God's promises have been fulfilled: "none remained without effect."

5. To come to someone by fate or destiny; to befall as a share. The verb can also express what happens to someone, what is assigned to them.
H5307L.origine: The root naphal expresses the idea of descending violently, losing balance or support. The verb can be used in the simple form ("to fall"), causative ("to make fall"), or reflexive ("to throw oneself"). The family of this word appears in several Semitic languages with the same fundamental meaning: to fall, to collapse, to tumble.
H5307L.emploi: The verb naphal appears about 90 times in the Hebrew Old Testament. The provided uses mainly show the figurative meaning: a word or a promise that "remains without effect" is a promise that does not fall, that does not become void. In Joshua 21:45, 23:14, and 1 Kings 8:56, the expression "remain without effect" affirms that all of God's good words to Israel have been fully accomplished. It is a positive way of saying: no promise has failed, has missed its goal. Elsewhere in the Bible, the verb also denotes death in battle, the fall of a city, prostration before God, or the arrival of fate upon someone.
H5307L.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's words never fall void. When Joshua declares that all of the Lord's promises have been fulfilled, it is to strengthen faith: God speaks, and what He says comes to fruition, nothing can stop His work. It is a guarantee that divine commitments to His people are secure and unshakeable.

sens: Make a tree fall, cut it down
Fall, collapse
Fall violently, crash down
Prostrate oneself, throw oneself to the ground
H5307M.detail:
1. To fell a tree, to make it fall for destruction or use: it is the action of striking a tree so that it collapses. In 2 Kings 3:19, the warriors "fell all the good trees" to destroy the resources of the enemy country.
2. To fall, to collapse from a great height or from an elevated position: the object or person loses balance and descends to the ground. In 2 Kings 6:5, the head of the axe "falls" into the water after coming loose from its handle.
3. To fall violently, to completely collapse, often in a violent or definitive manner: this describes total destruction. In Ezekiel 31:12, the majestic tree sees its branches "fall" in the mountains, an image of total loss of power.
4. To prostrate oneself, to throw oneself to the ground as a sign of submission or religious respect: it is a movement of the body downward, voluntary this time, often before someone greater.
H5307M.origine: The Hebrew root נפל denotes the action of tipping downward, losing one's position. It is related to the idea of downward movement, of losing balance. The word has been preserved in neighboring Semitic languages. In biblical Hebrew, derivatives are found that denote things that "fall" (branches, fruits) or that are "made to fall" (enemies, trees). It is a very basic word to express any movement downward.
H5307M.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the provided passages, always with the concrete meaning of to fell or to fall. In 2 Kings 3:19 and 2 Kings 3:25, it refers to felling trees as an act of military destruction. In 2 Kings 6:5, an axe "falls" after coming loose. In Ezekiel 31:12 and Zechariah 11:2, branches or the entire tree "fall" or are "felled" to symbolize the fall of great power. The word always denotes a physical action, never abstract in these examples.
H5307M.portee: This word reminds us that falling is a physical and spiritual reality: what is elevated can collapse. For the believer, it evokes the collapse of human power, the fragility of what seems unshakeable, and the importance of not erecting false powers. It also invites us to understand the act of prostration not as humiliation, but as a return to the truth of our position before God.

sens: Fall, collapse, be overturned
Fall mortally, perish violently
Prostrate oneself, humbly bow before someone
Rush upon, throw oneself against, attack
Miss, fail, not come to fruition
Present, lay down (a request, a prayer)
H5307N.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to fall to the ground, to physically collapse, to be overturned (a structure that collapses, an object that tumbles, a person who stumbles).
2. In a warrior or death context, "to fall" means to lose life violently: a soldier killed in battle, a condemned person.
3. To fall before someone means to prostrate oneself respectfully: one kneels or lies on the ground as a sign of submission or worship (a familiar image in the ancient East).
4. To rush upon someone means to attack suddenly: an army that throws itself upon the enemy, rain that pours down on the earth.
5. To miss or fail: an attempt that fails, a promise that does not come to fruition, a plan that goes awry.
6. In the provided passages (Jeremiah 42:2 and Daniel 9:18, 9:20), the word means "to present, to lay down, to submit": Daniel presents his supplications before God, as one would lay a petition at the feet of a king. It is the figurative sense of the concrete gesture of falling or lowering something.
H5307N.origine: The verb naphal comes from a very ancient Hebrew root meaning literally "to descend downward." It is related to the image of weight causing a fall, of inevitable descent: a ripe fruit falling from the tree, an object that is dropped. The same root has given rise to the term "nephel" (stillborn, aborted creature). The verb has many forms: Qal (the simple fall), Hiphil (to make fall, to overturn), Hithpael (to throw oneself, to prostrate). It is a very common verb in the Old Testament, with always vivid images.
H5307N.emploi: The verb naphal is one of the most frequent verbs in the Old Testament. It first appears in the strict sense: to fall literally, to collapse, to perish in battle (warrior or judgment contexts). Then it shifts to figurative meanings: to fall morally, to fail, to miss. In the provided texts from Jeremiah 42 and Daniel 9, the meaning becomes more refined: "to present" something (a supplication, a prayer) to someone more powerful. It is as if the supplicant "laid down" or "let fall" their request at God's feet in a sign of humility. The context and the prepositions that accompany the verb strongly affect its nuance: to fall with (perecer), to fall upon (to attack), to fall into the hand of (to be captured), to fall before (to prostrate oneself).
H5307N.portee: This word reminds us of the essential humility in prayer: the believer who presents their supplications symbolically kneels before God, acknowledging their total dependence and the disproportion between their weakness and divine power. It also invites meditation on the physical or moral fall of sin, and on the prostration that alone can precede restoration. For the evangelical reader, it is a verb that speaks of the path from downfall to humble lowering, the only path to grace.

sens: Lose balance and fall down
To prostrate oneself, to bow face down before someone or something
H5308.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to fall physically, to lose footing and collapse to the ground. This is the literal and concrete meaning of the word.
2. In a religious or respectful context, to fall takes on the meaning of prostrating oneself: one throws oneself to the ground as a sign of worship, submission, or homage. Daniel 2:46 is a perfect example: King Nebuchadnezzar "fell on his face" before Daniel, not by accident, but as an act of reverence. Similarly, in Daniel 3, to fall means to bow down to worship the golden statue: it is a voluntary act of submission and worship.
H5308.origine: The Aramaic verb נְפַל comes from a common Semitic root expressing movement downward, collapse, or fall. The corresponding Hebrew word, נָפַל, has exactly the same meaning and is used very broadly in the Old Testament for any physical or figurative fall. In the late Aramaic of the book of Daniel, the meaning of religious prostration has crystallized and dominates its usages.
H5308.emploi: The word appears only in the Aramaic books of the Old Testament: mainly Daniel (9 occurrences), and once in Ezra. In Daniel, it almost always describes prostration before an idol or royal authority (statues, king): it is an act of forced or voluntary worship. In Ezra 7:20, it means rather "to be necessary" or "to be required," a more abstract sense where to fall means to be needed, to be incumbent. The Segond translations vary: "to prostrate" predominates widely, but also "to fall" and "to be necessary" depending on the context.
H5308.portee: This word illustrates how a simple verb of physical movement becomes the expression of deep attitudes: prostration before a god reveals the heart of the worshiper. In Daniel, the three young Hebrews refuse to prostrate themselves, reminding the believer that true worship belongs to God alone. Physical falling can also evoke humility and recognition of one's smallness before the divine.

sens: stillborn child or one that did not survive birth
something without value or substance
a fate more favorable than the misery of a meaningless life
H5309.detail:
1. A miscarriage is a child that is born dead or dies immediately after birth, without having had the chance to live. It is the image of what has never truly existed: Job says he would have preferred to be a "hidden miscarriage," never to have been born rather than to suffer (Job 3:16).
2. By extension, a miscarriage refers to something weak, without strength, without substance — something as insignificant as an ephemeral creature. The psalmist wishes that the wicked "perish like a snail," never seeing the light, "like the miscarriage of a woman" (Psalms 58:9).
3. The miscarriage also becomes a measure of comparison to judge what is better: a miscarriage that has never lived is happier than a rich man who has accumulated a hundred sons and long years, but whose soul has never tasted satisfaction and who will have no burial (Ecclesiastes 6:3).
H5309.origine: The Hebrew word nèphel comes from a root that evokes what falls or escapes — like a fruit that falls from the tree before ripening. It is the image of what does not come to term, of what is incomplete or rejected. The word expresses the idea of futility and nothingness.
H5309.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in books of wisdom or lamentation. In Job 3:16, it expresses the character's desire to have never existed rather than to know suffering. In Psalms 58:9, it describes the wished fate of the wicked — that they collapse like things without substance. In Ecclesiastes 6:3, it becomes a moral reference point: even one who has never lived is happier than a man empty of satisfaction and deprived of funeral dignity. In all cases, the word expresses the idea that there are worse things than not existing.
H5309.portee: This word teaches the believer that true misfortune is not the absence of life, but a life empty, without contentment or dignity. It is an invitation to seek what truly fills the soul — what Ecclesiastes recognizes as one of the enigmas of human existence. The text urges us to reflect on what gives weight and meaning to our days.

sens: Reduce to pieces, shatter a fragile object
Destroy, pulverize a solid substance
Annihilate, crush an opponent or a kingdom
H5310A.detail:
1. To break primarily means to smash, shatter a fragile object: the jars that Gideon and his men held (Judges 7:19) were broken to release the light of their torches in the night; it is a destructive and violent act, but controlled.
2. The word can also describe the pulverization of a hard substance reduced to dust: the stones of the idols' altars were turned to dust (Isaiah 27:9), an image of their complete and irretrievable annihilation.
3. Figuratively, to break applies to the overwhelming domination of a power over its enemies: God breaks nations and kingdoms by His instrument of war (Jeremiah 51:20-22), an image of total victory and destruction of resistance.
H5310A.origine: The Hebrew verb naphats expresses the action of breaking, shattering with force. It comes from a root that paints the physical image of breaking and scattering: a broken thing disperses, reduces to fragments. The word appears mainly in contexts of war or divine judgment, where destruction is complete.
H5310A.emploi: This verb appears about 13 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used in the literal sense: breaking a jar, a vase (Judges 7:19, Jeremiah 22:28). Then it takes on a more powerful meaning in the oracles of judgment and descriptions of divine domination: breaking nations, kingdoms, peoples (Jeremiah 51:20-22, Psalms 2:9). In the prophets, to break describes the action of God who crushes idols and their worshipers, symbolizing the end of their power and pretension. The word intensifies the idea of destruction: what is broken cannot be restored.
H5310A.portee: This word reminds the reader that God holds absolute power over all that opposes Him: kingdoms, idols, human systems cannot withstand His judgment. For the believer, to break speaks of the fragility of the powers of the world and the final victory of God. It is also an invitation not to fear present powers: they are like breakable vessels in the hands of the Lord.

sens: To spread out in various directions, to disseminate
To scatter, to flee in all directions
To populate an area by gradually settling in it
H5310B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of spatial dispersion: people or things spread out here and there, disseminating. Thus, after the flood, Noah's sons and their descendants "populated" the whole earth by gradually dispersing across the continents (Genesis 9:19).
2. The word also describes flight or rout: when a force appears, people flee and disperse in all directions. Saul sees his army "dispersing" far from him in the face of the Philistine threat (1 Samuel 13:11), and the nations "disperse" at the voice of God (Isaiah 33:3).
3. In a context of restoration, "dispersed" refers to the scattered exiles: it is the future Messiah who will "gather the exiles of Israel" and collect the "dispersed" of Judah from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12).
H5310B.origine: The Hebrew root נפץ (naphats) evokes the idea of bursting and dissemination. It is related to the image of what breaks or scatters: like objects that disperse after a shock. The word appears mainly in historical and prophetic contexts to speak of population movements or flight in the face of a threat.
H5310B.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible provided. In Genesis 9:19, it describes the natural process of populating the earth after the flood. In 1 Samuel 13:11, it expresses military panic: the soldiers disperse in the face of the enemy. In Isaiah, the word is used twice: first to refer to the scattered exiles that the Messiah will gather (11:12), and then to describe how the nations flee before God (33:3). Its meaning varies slightly between a natural and progressive dispersion, a panicked flight, and a dispersion forced by exile.
H5310B.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer by reminding that God controls the movements of peoples and knows His scattered children. It offers hope: even when God's people are scattered far from their land, the Messiah has the power to gather and restore them. It is a promise of gathering and return.

sens: deluge or devastating torrent
violent and sudden assault
manifestation of divine power
H5311.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a flood or violent inundation — a mass of water that pours forth with force and ravages everything in its path. In Isaiah 30:30, the flood is among the instruments of divine judgment, alongside the storm and hail: it is a raw force of nature, destructive and irresistible.
2. It can also evoke any sudden and violent assault or surge — anything that comes upon you unexpectedly and overwhelms you. The biblical context makes it an image of punishment: it is God who sends this devastating flood.
3. Figuratively, it is a striking manifestation of divine power in action. In Isaiah 30:30, the flood belongs to the arsenal of eschatological judgment — the moment when God shows His absolute authority through terrifying and irrefutable signs.
H5311.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing the idea of gushing or violent overflow. It refers to the raw image of the flood — what swells, overflows, inundates — with a connotation of suddenness and destructive power. This root is rare in the Old Testament, highlighting the exceptional and dramatic nature of the phenomenon described.
H5311.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:30. This unique usage places it in an eschatological context: the prophet Isaiah describes the moment when God will punish the enemies of Israel. The flood is listed as one of the manifestations of divine judgment, alongside flame, storm, and hailstones — all images of overwhelming power and inevitable destruction.
H5311.portee: This word reminds us that God's anger is real and terrible, but also that God commands all of nature. For the reader, the image of the inevitable flood invites serious consideration of the prophet's warnings and the reality of divine judgment. It is a call to align oneself with God rather than against Him.

sens: to move outward, to leave a place
to bring someone or something out, to remove
to make known publicly, to promulgate
H5312.detail:
1. To go out simply means to leave a place to go outside or elsewhere. When the sentence is published (Daniel 2:13), it "goes out" — it is announced and spreads. When Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are called, they "go out" from the midst of the fire (Daniel 3:26): they withdraw from the furnace where they were thrown.
2. To remove expresses the action of taking something out of a place to transport it elsewhere. King Cyrus had the utensils brought from Jerusalem removed from the temple in Babylon (Ezra 5:14): he took them away and returned them. This is also the sense of the vessel that is "removed" for use (Daniel 5:2).
3. To publish or promulgate: when a sentence "goes out," it becomes public and official. Daniel went out of his house to meet the chief of the guards (Daniel 2:14) — he voluntarily presented himself outside.
H5312.origine: The Aramaic verb נְפַק (nepaq) expresses the simple movement of going out, of emission, of crossing a boundary or threshold. It is mainly used in the accounts of the Babylonian captivity and in the book of Daniel. The word always implies a spatial limit or an initial condition from which one escapes or from which something is drawn.
H5312.emploi: The verb appears 9 times, mainly in the books of Ezra and Daniel (the end of the Aramaic Old Testament). It is used in two registers: physical movement (soldiers going out, men called to leave a place) and the movement of objects (removal of vessels from the temple). In Ezra, it often refers to the removal of sacred objects: Nebuchadnezzar took them from Jerusalem, and King Cyrus removes them from Babylon to return them. In Daniel, it is the action of going outside or making known (the sentence that goes out, meaning that it is promulgated). The meaning always remains: to cross a boundary, to move from one state or place to another.
H5312.portee: This simple yet rich verb reminds us that the temple vessels, symbols of God's presence among His people, were taken into exile but are not held captive — God brings them back. For the believer, it speaks of liberation and restoration: what was held back returns to its place, and those threatened by death are called to come out of danger.

sens: expenditure of money necessary to accomplish a project
financial cost to bear for a construction or enterprise
H5313.detail:
1. The word concretely denotes the money that must be spent to accomplish something: the costs of constructing the temple. It is everything that the project costs. In Ezra 6:4, we speak of the "costs" of the reconstruction of the temple, meaning the total amount that the king's house must pay.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the financial effort and material commitment that an authority or community must undertake for a given work. In Ezra 6:8, the king of Persia orders that "the costs" be "paid exactly" to the elders of the Jews: it is the money taken from the royal treasury so that the construction of the temple does not stop.
H5313.origine: The Aramaic word comes from a root meaning "to go out" or "to be taken away." The costs are literally what "goes out" of the treasury, what is "extracted" or "spent": the money that leaves the coffers to be used. It is a very natural image: expenditure is what goes away, what disappears from the assets to go to work.
H5313.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Aramaic in the book of Ezra, in chapters 6:4 and 6:8. It refers each time to financing the reconstruction of the temple after the exile. The context is that of the decree of the king of Persia ordering that the costs of construction be taken from the tributes and paid regularly to the workers and elders. The word emphasizes the idea that someone — here the king — must bear the financial cost of the project.
H5313.portee: For the believer, this passage shows that even in exile, God provides for the needs of His people by stirring the heart of a pagan king to finance the reconstruction of the temple. It teaches that God never abandons His project and that He can use the resources of the world to accomplish His work.

sens: To catch one's breath, to regain one's breath after exertion
To interrupt work to recover
To regain strength and vigor
To cease being active, to remain inactive
H5314.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the physical act of catching one's breath: after working hard, one stops to breathe and recover. This is what one feels after exhausting oneself and finally releasing their effort (Exodus 23:12, where both the slave and the donkey must have rest).
2. More broadly, it means to interrupt one's work, to intentionally cease working to allow the body and mind to recover. God Himself, after six days of creation, rested on the seventh day: not because He was tired, but He ceased His creative activity (Exodus 31:17).
3. Rest also brings back strength and vigor: one who rests is no longer weakened, they are revitalized.
4. Finally, it is the state of inactivity, calm, and absence of labor: one no longer works, remaining in restorative idleness.
H5314.origine: The root literally means "to breathe" or "to take breath": the basic image is that of breathing resuming after being out of breath. The Hebrew word naphaš also refers to the soul, life, vital breath — that which animates and gives vigor. By taking on the meaning of "to rest," the verb refers to this fundamental need that every living being has to regain its breath and strength.
H5314.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Old Testament, always in a context of mandatory or beneficial rest. In Exodus 23:12, it refers to the rest of the seventh day: everyone, whether slave or donkey, must cease work to rest — it is a right, almost a holy obligation. In Exodus 31:17, God Himself rests after creation: not out of fatigue, but to sanctify rest as a divine principle. The text in 2 Samuel 16:14, where David and his escort rest during their flight, shows rest as physical recovery. The word always denotes a salutary interruption of work.
H5314.portee: This word reminds us that rest is not a luxury or laziness, but a necessity created by God: He instituted the seventh day so that everyone — master, slave, beast — could catch their breath. For the Christian, it is an invitation to respect rest as an act of obedience and trust: not resting is to ignore the divine wisdom that knows that every living being needs to stop in order to continue.

sens: That which breathes, the principle of life in a living being
The person themselves, the individual considered in their entirety
The seat of desires, appetites, and hunger
The seat of feelings, emotions, and passions
The seat of thought, will, and character
Life itself, that which animates the body
H5315G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates that which breathes within us: the living substance, the breath that animates the body. This is what is called the soul, distinct from the body but inseparable from it in earthly life. When Jacob arrives in Bethlehem (Genesis 35:18), Rachel "gives up her soul" in giving birth to Benjamin: her soul leaves her body with her last breath.
2. Very often, "soul" simply means "I," "you," "he" — the whole person. In 1 Samuel 18:1, David and Jonathan have such a strong friendship that "the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David": this indicates that Jonathan loved David with all his being.
3. The soul is the seat of hunger and desire: "My soul longs for the judgments of the Lord" (Psalm 19:8). It expresses what we need or want, what drives us to act.
4. The soul feels emotions: it rejoices, grieves, and consumes. When David "pours out tears and fasts," it is to show that "his soul" suffers (Psalm 69:11). The soul can also hate, as when God says, "My soul hates your feasts" (Isaiah 1:14): this is deep disgust.
5. The soul thinks and deliberates: "Take care and keep your soul diligently" (Deuteronomy 4:9) invites us to watch over what we retain and meditate upon. It is the seat of intelligence and judgment.
6. Ultimately, the soul is simply life, that which keeps a being alive. In Leviticus 17:11, "the life of the flesh is in the blood": the soul and the blood are linked, one does not exist without the other.
H5315G.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to breathe" or "to pant." The soul is therefore primarily the breath, the respiration — that which comes out of the mouth and proves that one is alive. All beings that breathe have a soul: humans, animals, creatures. The same root underlies the words "nephesh" (soul), "nishmat" (breath), and "nishmé" (respiration). This image of breath is very ancient: it expresses the idea that life is something invisible and immaterial, present in the body but not reduced to it.
H5315G.emploi: The word "soul" (nephesh) appears more than 230 times in the Old Testament, especially in historical, poetic, and prophetic books. It primarily designates the living being endowed with breath: humans and animals (Genesis 1:30). Very quickly, it takes on the meaning of the person themselves, the individual in all their uniqueness. It can express bodily appetites (Deuteronomy 12:20: "If your soul desires to eat meat"), emotions (1 Samuel 30:6: "bitterness in the soul"), loyalty (1 Samuel 18:1-3: the covenant between David and Jonathan). It also expresses life that can be taken away (Leviticus 17:11: "the life of the flesh is in the blood"), and the total commitment of the person to God (Deuteronomy 6:5: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul"). The word does not really change meaning: it is the perspective that changes according to the context — sometimes we look at physical life, sometimes the personal being, sometimes emotional or moral commitment.
H5315G.portee: For the Christian reader, "soul" designates the living unity of the person — not a detachable part of the body, but the living person in all their integrity. When Jesus asks (drawing from Deuteronomy 6:5) to love God "with all your soul," it is asking for total commitment, from the heart as well as from the mind. This word also reminds us that God knows and loves each person individually, in the secret of their inner life — each one is a unique soul before God. Finally, the soul speaks to us of the fragility and preciousness of life: it can be preserved or lost, nourished or starved, which is why God cares for it and invites us to take care of it.

sens: The principle of life that animates a living being, what makes it breathe and exist
Life itself, what can be lost, threatened, or saved
The individual person, the human being in its entirety
The seat of desires, appetites, and inclinations
The center of emotions and passions
The seat of thought, will, and character
H5315H.detail:
1. The soul is primarily what breathes, the vital breath that makes a being alive. Genesis 1:30 speaks of everything that has the breath of life within it: it is the soul that distinguishes an animal or a person from a dead thing.
2. By extension, the soul refers to the concrete life of a person — that which can be lost, endangered, or saved. When Elijah "saves his life" in 1 Kings 19:3, he flees to escape death. This is a very physical and immediate sense.
3. The soul can also mean the person themselves, the individual as a whole. Saying "my life" or "your life" in Hebrew often amounts to saying "me" or "you".
4. The soul is the seat of desires and appetites: what we want, what attracts us. Proverbs 19:16 refers to the soul as the center of what directs us.
5. It is also the heart of emotions and passions — joy, fear, anger, love — everything that stirs our inner being.
6. Finally, the soul is linked to the activity of thought, will, and character: it is through it that we reflect, decide, and act according to our values.
H5315H.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to breathe." The soul is therefore literally "that which breathes" — the vital breath. This image is found in all ancient languages: breath is the sign of life. In Hebrew, the same word also denotes desire and appetite, for what lives desires to survive and be nourished. This is why the soul is the center not only of physical breath but also of all inner life.
H5315H.emploi: This word appears 180 times in the Old Testament — it is one of the most important. It appears mainly in the historical books (1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings) and in the wisdom books (Proverbs). In the law (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy), the soul is what costs a ransom in the case of murder: "life for life." In narratives, it generally refers to a person's life in danger — one flees to "save their soul," one plots to "take someone's soul." The word can also denote appetite or desire: a soul that is hungry. Thus, depending on the contexts, the word oscillates between the very concrete sense of "life" and the deeper sense of "person" or "interiority."
H5315H.portee: This word teaches us that in biblical thought, we are not a soul imprisoned in a body, but a unified and living person. The soul is not a part of us detachable from the rest: it is ourselves, our whole life, what animates us. For the Christian, this means that God is interested in our entire person, not just an abstract spiritual part. This is also why Scripture speaks of "saving a soul": it is about saving the whole person, in what is deepest within them.

sens: What breathes and lives within us, the living essence of a creature or person
The person themselves, the individual
The seat of desires, appetites, and hunger
The seat of feelings, emotions, and passions
The will and personal conscience
Life itself, what sustains a living being
H5315I.detail:
1. What breathes and lives within us: the Hebrew word literally designates "that which breathes" — it is the living essence, the breath that animates a creature. This is why it is found for both animals and humans, wherever there is life (Genesis 1 in the original version). This is the primary image: breath, what differentiates a living being from a corpse.

2. The person themselves: the soul does not refer to a detachable part of us, but to us as a whole. When one says "my soul bless you" (Genesis 27:4), it is like saying "I bless you with all my being," "I myself bless you." 

3. The seat of desires and appetite: the soul expresses what is hungry, what seeks to be satisfied. Jeremiah 2:24 speaks of the she-ass "panting in the heat of her passion" — her intense desire is a matter of the soul. This is why we say "a hungry soul." 

4. The seat of emotions and passions: the soul is the place where joy, sorrow, hatred, love are born. When Isaac says to Jacob, "may my soul bless you" (Genesis 27:19), it is a gesture of the heart. Leviticus 26:30 also expresses the revulsion of the whole being: "my soul will abhor you." 

5. The will and conscience: the soul is also the center of our decisions and personal choices. In the vows of Numbers 30, "making a vow upon one's soul" means committing one's free will, making a personal resolution.

6. Life itself: the soul is what sustains life. Leviticus 7:18 speaks of one who "eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of thanksgiving that same day" — it is the idea that the soul persists, that the person exists. It is the vital principle that can be threatened, that can be in danger.
H5315I.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to breathe" or "to pant." The image is that of vital breath: what animates a being and makes it alive. In biblical Hebrew, the soul is never an immaterial reality floating above the body — it is the whole person as they live, breathe, desire, feel, and act. This concept reflects a view of humanity as an indivisible whole, very different from Greek philosophy which would divide soul and body. Other words from the same family express the idea of breathing, sighing, or wishing.
H5315I.emploi: This word is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible (126 occurrences provided). It appears mainly in the books of the Law (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) to express the person who makes a vow or a religious act, and in the Psalms and wisdom books to describe emotional and spiritual states. In Isaac and Jacob, the soul is that which blesses or curses — it is the person in their personal commitment. In the laws of Leviticus, "to defile one's soul" or "to afflict one's soul" (through fasting) means to personally submit to God's will. In the Psalms, the soul cries out to God, it loses confidence, it is in danger — it is the most vivid expression of distress or personal prayer. The meaning varies: sometimes it is the person themselves, sometimes it is the seat of emotion, sometimes it is the life that one risks losing. This richness shows that the soul, for biblical Hebrew, is all that we are and all that we feel.
H5315I.portee: Understanding what the Bible means by "soul" heals the false idea of a world divided between matter and spirit. God is interested in you — in your whole person, your desires, your feelings, your choices — not just in an immaterial part of you. When the Bible speaks of afflicting one's soul (fasting), it calls for engaging your whole will. And when a Psalmist cries, "my soul seeks you," it expresses that you are created to seek God with all your being. It is a call to personal integrity: you cannot serve God "in spirit" without engaging your body, your concrete choices, and your real life.

sens: Principle of life that animates a living being, making it capable of breathing and feeling
Individual person, human being considered as a unit
Life itself, the existence of a creature
Seat of desires, appetites, and feelings
Center of thought and will
Totality of a person's being, in its physical and spiritual dimensions
H5315J.detail:
1. The soul is primarily what gives life to a creature: it is the breath, the vital force that animates the body. The word comes from a root that means "to breathe." This is why Joshua 11:11 says that they "devoted all who breathed": every soul that breathes is a life.

2. The word then designates the person itself, the individual counted as a unit. Exodus 12:16 speaks of "the food of each person": each soul is a eater, an actor. Similarly, Numbers 31:40 counts "sixteen thousand persons": each soul counts as a head.

3. The soul is also the life that can be lost, that is at risk or that is given. When we talk about saving a soul or delivering a soul to death, we are speaking of someone's very existence.

4. It is the home of desires and appetites: a hungry soul, a soul that desires. Proverbs 19:2 says "a soul without knowledge is not good": it is the person in their desire to know.

5. The soul is also the center of thought and will: it is where we reflect, decide, love, or hate. It is the deep "self" of each being.

6. In the most complete sense, the soul is the whole being, the living totality of a person — not just their body, but their body-person animated by life, desire, thought, and will.
H5315J.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to breathe" or "to gasp." The starting image is that of breath: what breathes is what lives. In Hebrew, the soul is not separated from the body as in Greek philosophy; it is the whole living and breathing person. The word appears throughout the Hebrew Scriptures to speak of life, person, appetite, desire — in short, of the living being in all its dimensions.
H5315J.emploi: The word appears 83 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and the historical narratives (Joshua, Samuel, Kings). It is used very concretely: counting souls (number of people), feeding souls (giving food), striking souls (killing people). In Levitical law, "a soul that sins" refers to a responsible person who has violated the Law. In Proverbs, the soul becomes the seat of feelings (hunger, fatigue, pride). The meaning varies little: it is always the living person, accountable for their actions and capable of desiring, thinking, and suffering.
H5315J.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that in biblical thought, we are total living beings, not divided into opposing parts. Our life, our desires, our responsibility, our thought are all connected. When Jesus calls to "save one's soul," it is not to flee the world: it is to preserve one's whole life in the presence of God. It also invites us to respect each person as a "soul" — a unique, living being who matters before the Lord.

sens: living creature that breathes
living being endowed with movement
creature endowed with life in the blood
H5315K.detail:
1. The word primarily designates anything that breathes, any animated creature — it is the vital breath that makes the difference between a living being and dead matter. In Genesis 1:20-21, God commands the waters to produce living animals, fish, and birds: these are beings that breathe and move.
2. It is also the living being as a whole, the animal as a complete creature. On the sixth day (Genesis 1:24), God tells the earth to produce animals according to their kind — livestock, reptiles, land animals. The word encompasses all this diversity.
3. The Bible emphasizes: it is a living creature whose life resides in the blood. This detail is highlighted in Genesis 9:10-16: the rainbow is a sign of the covenant that God makes with every animal of the earth and air after the flood. The life of the blood is what makes the animal precious in God's eyes.
H5315K.origine: The word comes from the root that means "to breathe," "to blow." This is why it first describes what has vital breath within itself. In Hebrew, the same word is also used to designate the human soul, heart, will, appetite — everything that makes a person live from the inside. Here, in the creation narrative, it is applied to animal creatures: they too have this breath, this life, which makes them precious.
H5315K.emploi: The word appears mainly in chapters 1-2 of Genesis, during the creation narrative. God commands the waters and the earth to produce living animals (1:20, 1:21, 1:24). Moses also mentions that the land animal has a living soul (2:19). Later, in Genesis 9:10-16, after the flood, God establishes his covenant with every animal of the earth: the word returns four times to emphasize that each living creature is part of the covenant. Finally, the purity laws in Leviticus 11:10 and 11:46 speak of living animals that should not be eaten — they have blood flowing in them. Ezekiel 47:9 mentions living animals near the river of the temple. In all cases, the animal is a breathing creature, endowed with life, worthy of respect because it carries within it the breath of God.
H5315K.portee: This word reminds us that animal life comes from God and not from us. Creatures are not mere objects: they have a vital breath, a soul, an existence that God created and deemed good. The covenant of Genesis 9 includes animals, showing that they are part of the world that God governs and protects. This invites the Christian to see creatures with respect, as living beings and not merely as resources to exploit.

sens: That which breathes in us, life itself, the breath of the living
The person, the individual, what we call 'I'
The seat of desire, appetite, hunger
The seat of emotions, feelings, and passions
The will, that which wants and chooses
Mental activity, thought and reflection
H5315L.detail:
1. The soul is primarily that which breathes, that which gives life to the body — the living being itself. It is this breath that God breathes into man. In Hebrew, the word literally means 'that which breathes' or 'the breathing one'.

2. The soul also refers to the whole person: you, me, someone. When it says 'my soul will be satisfied' (Jeremiah 50:19), it is not just speaking of a mystical part of oneself, but of the whole self, of the complete person.

3. The soul is the seat of desire and appetite. It hungers, it thirsts, it covets. 'Why do you labor for what does not satisfy?' asks Isaiah: he speaks of the soul that is never satisfied with what it covets (Ecclesiastes 6:7).

4. The soul feels emotions, feelings, passions — joy, sadness, anger. It is in it that the movements of the heart arise. When the enemy says 'My vengeance will be satisfied', he expresses a passion of his soul (Exodus 15:9).

5. The soul wants, chooses, desires. It is the center of the will, of what we truly decide. 'At your pleasure' means 'as your soul desires': you eat grapes if that is what you want (Deuteronomy 23:24).

6. The soul thinks, reflects, knows. It is the activity of the mind, the seat of consciousness and understanding.
H5315L.origine: The Hebrew word נֶפֶשׁ (néphesh) comes from a root that means 'to breathe', 'to blow'. Its primary image is therefore breath, respiration, that which gives life. In biblical Hebrew, 'soul' rarely speaks of an immaterial entity separate from the body: it rather designates the living person in its entirety, always linked to physical life. The word is close to the Greek concept of 'psyche' but without the same philosophical weight: the Hebrew soul is embodied, it lives, it desires, it acts in the material world.
H5315L.emploi: This word appears 45 times in the Old Testament, particularly in the Wisdom literature (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Job) and among the prophets. It is used in two main ways: the soul as life or person ('to save one's soul', 'to lose one's soul'), and the soul as the seat of desire and appetite. In the provided usages, it is mostly expressing appetite and desire: the hungry soul of the thief who steals to eat (Proverbs 6:30), the soul that delights or is satisfied (Isaiah 55:2, Jeremiah 50:19), the soul never satisfied with its cravings (Ecclesiastes 6:7). It can also simply mean 'person' or 'myself', sometimes rendered by the pronoun 'self' in the Segond.
H5315L.portee: Understanding that the soul is not in us a hidden immaterial divine spark within the flesh, but rather our whole person — what we today call our 'living being' — helps us see that God loves us entirely, body and spirit. It also recognizes that our desires, appetites, and emotions are real and important in God's eyes; He is not ashamed of them. But the soul hungry for what does not nourish will never find rest: this is why the prophet calls us to feed on what truly satisfies (Isaiah 55:2).

sens: deceased person, corpse
lifeless body of a man or woman
ritual impurity caused by contact with a corpse
H5315M.detail:
1. The word designates a person who has ceased to live, the corpse or the lifeless body. In Leviticus 21:11, the priest may not approach any 'dead' person so as not to become unclean: it refers to the inert human body.
2. More broadly, it is the physical body of a deceased person, considered in its materiality. Numbers 19:11 explicitly speaks of 'a dead person, any human body': death has transformed the living person into a body that could cause impurity.
3. By extension, contact or proximity with a corpse leads to ritual impurity. Numbers 5:2 commands to send away from the camp 'anyone... who is unclean because of a dead person', meaning contaminated by contact with it. This impurity is not moral, but cultic: it prevents participation in sacred acts until purification.
H5315M.origine: The Hebrew word נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh) primarily means 'that which breathes', 'the living being'. In the provided usages here, it has a specific and restricted meaning: it designates not the living person or their soul, but the dead person, their corpse. This is a particular usage of the word explained by the context of the Israelite cultic system: before the laws of purity, the corpse is named by a word that has other meanings elsewhere in the Bible.
H5315M.emploi: In these passages (Leviticus 19-22 and Numbers 5-19), nephesh in the sense of 'death, corpse' appears about 13 times. The context is always that of the law of ritual purity in Israel. The priests, notably the high priests, cannot touch or approach a dead person without becoming unclean for a given time (seven days according to Numbers 19:11). Even the Nazirite, consecrated to God by a special vow, is subject to this rule (Numbers 6:6-11). The word also appears to indicate that the entire people must keep away from corpses or must be purified from them. This is a practice of the worship of the God of Israel: the corpse, associated with decomposition and the absence of life, represented a form of impurity that had to be managed by specific rites.
H5315M.portee: This notion of ritual purity concerning the dead shows that the people of Israel had to manage their relationship to the sacred in a very concrete way, through their bodies and actions. For today's believer, this reminds us that death remains a reality to be respected and integrated into religious life: life and death are distinct realms in God's plan. It is also an indication that God desires His people to live under the sign of life, separated from the realities of decomposition and nothingness— a prophetic call to choose blessing and life rather than cursing and death.

sens: The vital breath, that which animates a living being and keeps it alive
The person itself, the individual in its entirety
The seat of desires, appetites, and bodily needs
The seat of emotions, feelings, and passions
The activity of thought and will, the interiority of the person
H5315N.detail:
1. The vital breath: nèphesh primarily refers to that which breathes, the living principle within us. It is the very essence of animal and human life — what makes a creature alive rather than dead. In Psalms 69:2, the psalmist cries, "Save me, O God! For the waters threaten my life": he asks God to save his soul from the immediate danger of death.
2. The whole person: nèphesh often refers to the person itself, the complete individual — what is called the living being. It is "I", "you", "he" in all its reality.
3. The seat of appetites: the word also evokes the desires of the body — hunger, thirst, material needs. It is the soul that hungers, that desires, that wants to be satisfied.
4. The seat of emotions: the soul is the place of deep feelings — joy, sadness, fear, love, anger. It is through the soul that one experiences passions.
5. Personal interiority: nèphesh finally represents mental and moral life — thought, will, character — all that constitutes the person in its spiritual and moral essence.
H5315N.origine: The word nèphesh comes from a root that evokes breath, respiration, breath. The starting image is very physical: what breathes is alive, what stops breathing dies. From this comes the broad meaning of the word — first biological life, then gradually the whole person in all its dimensions: body, desires, emotions, intelligence. It is a key word in Hebrew thought, which does not separate the soul from the body as Greek philosophy would, but sees the human being as a living unity animated by this divine breath.
H5315N.emploi: The word nèphesh is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Old Testament. It also appears in passages where it is translated as "life": in Psalms 69:2, the psalmist asks that his nèphesh be saved from death (the waters threatening to drown); in Psalms 105:18, it is Joseph's nèphesh that is put in chains — that is, Joseph himself, his person. The context determines the nuance: in the face of danger, it is life that one fears to lose; in a personal relationship, it is the person that is targeted; in the cry of the heart, it is the emotion of the soul. The word thus covers the entire living being, from the biological to the moral.
H5315N.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the Bible sees the human being in a holistic way, not fragmented: there are no separate parts (body on one side, soul on the other), but a whole person, animated by the life that God gives. Recognizing that my nèphesh — my soul, my whole being — depends on God and that it is He who keeps it from death is the foundation of trust and faith.

sens: region of Judea
area occupied by the tribe of Manasseh
H5316G.detail: Naphath is a mountainous region of the Promised Land. It is mentioned in the context of the land distribution among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
H5316G.origine: The Hebrew word נֶ֫פֶת (naphath) literally means "height" or "elevated region", which well describes the geography of this territory. It comes from a root denoting the elevation of the terrain.
H5316G.emploi: Naphath appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 17:11, in the description of the borders and cities assigned to the tribe of Manasseh after entering Canaan. It designates a particular region of the territory of Manasseh, probably a mountainous or hilly area.

sens: coastal region of northern Israel, also called Dor
H5316H.detail:
1. Naphath is another designation for the region of Dor, located in northern Israel, near the Mediterranean coast. It appears notably when listing the cities conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:23) and when listing the governors established by Solomon (1 Kings 4:11).
2. The name Naphath comes from a Hebrew root meaning "height" or "elevated region". It is a variant or nickname for Dor, a major coastal city in northern Israel. This dual name reflects the strategic importance of this place in ancient Israel.
H5316H.origine: The name Naphath comes from a Hebrew root meaning "height" or "elevated region". It is a variant or nickname for Dor, a major coastal city in northern Israel. This dual name reflects the strategic importance of this place in ancient Israel.
H5316H.emploi: Naphath appears twice in the Old Testament. It is mentioned in the list of defeated Canaanite kings during the conquest (Joshua 12:23), and then in the enumeration of the twelve administrative districts established by King Solomon, of which Naphath of Dor constituted a major economic and strategic sector (1 Kings 4:11).
