These two occurrences highlight the enduring importance of this region through the periods of judgment (Joshua) and stable monarchy (Solomon).

sens: sweet substance produced by bees
honey that flows from the combs
sweetness, pleasant flavor
that which is sweet to the ear or heart
H5317.detail: 1. Honey is the sweet, golden substance that bees produce and store in the combs of their hive. It is a precious and tasty food in ancient Israel (Proverbs 24:13). 2. The word particularly evokes honey that flows, that "drips" from the combs, an image of generosity and abundance (Psalms 19:11: "sweeter than honey, than that which flows from the combs"). 3. By its exquisite taste, honey becomes the biblical symbol of sweetness, pleasure, and delight: the Word of God itself is compared to something sweeter than honey (Psalms 19:11). 4. Honey also denotes that which charms or seduces the heart — thus the words of the strange woman "drip honey" (Proverbs 5:3), meaning they seduce by their deceptive sweetness, although they lead to bitterness.
H5317.origine: The Hebrew word nophet comes from a root meaning "to flow" or "to drip": it denotes that which flows, that drips drop by drop. This reflects the image of honey dripping from the combs of the hive, slowly and generously. Honey was in antiquity a highly valued product, a source of natural sweetness before the existence of refined sugar.
H5317.emploi: The word honey appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs three times, Psalms once, Song of Songs once). It primarily denotes literal honey, a nutritious and pleasant food: the hungry find it "sweet" even when alone (Proverbs 27:7), while the satisfied disdain it. But the Bible also uses it metaphorically: the divine Word surpasses the sweetness of honey (Psalms 19:11), and the flattering words of seduction have the deceptive sweetness of honey that flows (Proverbs 5:3; Song of Songs 4:11). The word always emphasizes an experience of pleasant flavor or seductive allure.
H5317.portee: Honey reminds us that the Word of God is not only true but pleasant to receive and meditate upon: it nourishes the soul far beyond any earthly riches. At the same time, the Bible warns us that honey can seduce or deceive: we must discern between true divine sweetness and deceptive words that shine like honey but lead to bitterness. This word invites us to taste the goodness of God (Psalms 34:9).

sens: A water spring located at the border between the territories of Judah and Benjamin
A geographical landmark to delineate tribal lands
H5318.detail:
1. Nephthoach is a spring or fountain of water that marks a specific location at the boundary of the territories of Judah and Benjamin. The Hebrew name literally means "opening," a natural image of a spring that bursts forth from the ground. It is located northwest of Jerusalem and appears twice in the description of the borders of these two tribes (Joshua 15:9 and Joshua 18:15).
2. This spring serves as a fixed and recognizable landmark for tracing the territorial limits between the two tribes. Like many permanent springs, it constitutes a stable reference point that the ancient Israelites could locate and use to precisely define who belonged to Judah and who belonged to Benjamin.
H5318.origine: The Hebrew name נֶפְתּוֹחַ (nephtoach) means "opening" or "that which opens." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of opening or splitting. The name aptly describes a water spring: a place where water "opens" or bursts forth from the ground. It is a descriptive name given to the location for its obvious geographical character.
H5318.emploi: Nephthoach appears only twice in the Bible, both in Joshua, in the context of tribal boundaries. In Joshua 15:9, it marks a key point of the southwestern boundary of Judah, between the summit of the mountain and Baala (Kirjath-Jearim). In Joshua 18:15, it is a similar landmark for the southern boundary of Benjamin. In both cases, the spring serves as a stopping point or turning point in the boundary line, indicating that it was a well-known and easily identifiable location for the Israelite surveyors.

sens: Close combat between two opponents seeking to overthrow each other
Intense effort to overcome resistance or an obstacle
Competition, rivalry between two individuals
H5319.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a close combat where two fighters attempt to overthrow or master each other: it is the physical image of wrestling, that of wrestlers (Genesis 30:8).
2. In a figurative sense, it evokes the vigorous effort to overcome a difficulty, to resist an opposing force. Rachel uses this word to describe her fierce competition with her sister Leah: she is not speaking of a fight, but of an intense rivalry where each seeks to prevail by any means (Genesis 30:8).
3. The word also carries the idea of personal conflict, of tension between two beings who oppose each other for the same cause or good.
H5319.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to turn, to evade, to dodge." The image is that of the body turning away, bending, twisting to escape or to master the opponent. This root evokes the movements of one who wrestles, who twists to escape or to conquer.
H5319.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 30:8. Rachel, having been barren for a long time, sees her servant Bilhah give her a second son. Jealous of her sister Leah, who already has four children, Rachel cries victory and names the newborn Nephthali — this name literally meaning "my struggles" — to commemorate her winning rivalry with Leah. This context shows that the struggle here is less physical than personal: it is the competition between two sisters for motherhood and the love of their husband.
H5319.portee: This word reminds us that the life of faith is not free from inner conflicts and human rivalries. It also shows how God incorporates even our personal battles, our jealousies, our efforts to prevail, into His plan: He brings forth a tribe of Israel from these fraternal struggles. For the believer, this invites recognition that God also uses our tensions and trials to accomplish His purpose.

sens: Egyptian people descended from Naphtuh
H5320.detail: The Naphtuhim are an Egyptian people mentioned in biblical genealogies as descendants of Naphtuh. They appear alongside other peoples from Egypt (Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Pathrusim, Casluhim, Caphtorim) in the list of nations founded after the flood.
H5320.origine: The name Naphtuhim literally means "openings," probably alluding to a region or geographical feature of Egypt, perhaps Lower Egypt. The precise origin of the term remains obscure, but it clearly designates a distinct Egyptian group in the table of nations.
H5320.emploi: The Naphtuhim are mentioned twice in Scripture, always in the context of the genealogy of peoples: first in Genesis 10:13, and a second time in 1 Chronicles 1:11, which repeats the same list. These two passages merely enumerate them among the Egyptian descendants without providing additional details about their history or territory.

sens: Son of Jacob and Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid
Israelite tribe descended from Nephthali
Territory allocated to the tribe of Nephthali in the Promised Land
H5321G.detail:
1. Nephthali is the fifth son of Jacob, born of Bilhah, the maidservant that Rachel gave to Jacob to bear children in her place. Rachel herself names the child saying: "I have wrestled mightily with my sister, and have prevailed" (Genesis 30:8) — his name means "wrestling" or "he who has wrestled." He is the brother of Dan, born of the same mother, and the half-brother of all Jacob's other sons.
2. The tribe of Nephthali is one of the twelve tribes of Israel, constituted by the descendants of this son of Jacob. It was numerous: in the desert census, it counted over fifty-three thousand men (Numbers 1:43). Its chiefs and princes are named in the tribal records, and it participated in the collective life of Israel, particularly during wars or major gatherings.
3. The territory of Nephthali extended to the north of the Promised Land, a hilly region with fortified cities (Joshua 19:32-39). Some Levitical cities were established there for the priests (Joshua 21:6). This region witnessed significant events: it is the territory of Jael and Deborah, and later the one that Isaiah calls "the land of Naphtali" in his prophecy about the people sitting in darkness (Isaiah 8:23).
H5321G.origine: The name Nephthali literally means "wrestling" or "he who wrestles," derived from a Hebrew root evoking struggle, combat, or rivalry. Rachel, in naming her son, expresses her symbolic victory in the rivalry with her sister Leah for giving children to Jacob. This sense of struggle or competition remains attached to the name throughout biblical history.
H5321G.emploi: Nephthali first appears as a person (the newborn child in Genesis 30:8), and then primarily as a tribe constituted by his descendants. All other biblical usages — a total of 46 references — refer either to the tribe in genealogical lists and censuses (Numbers 1-26), or its territory in the Promised Land (Joshua 19), or its participation in the life of Israel (wars, offerings at the Tabernacle in Numbers 7, exile in 2 Kings 15:29). The tribe occupies the north of Canaan and is featured in the prophetic prophecies of Isaiah and Ezekiel. Its importance remains consistent in the history of Israel from the desert to the exile.

sens: son of Jacob and Bilhah
tribe of Israel descended from Naphtali
mountainous territory in northern Israel assigned to this tribe
H5321H.detail: 1. Naphtali is one of the twelve sons of Jacob, born to Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant. His name means "struggle" or "fight," recalling the rivalry between the sisters for offspring. 2. After entering Canaan, the descendants of Naphtali form an important tribe of Israel, known for their warrior spirit and mobilization for major national battles, as seen in Judges 4:6 where Deborah summons "the children of Naphtali" alongside Barak against Sisera's army. 3. The territory of Naphtali extends in northern Israel, a mountainous and fertile region around the Sea of Galilee, with fortified cities like Kedesh-Naphtali, which would later become a refuge and a Levitical center.
H5321H.origine: The name Naphtali comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to struggle" or "to fight." According to Genesis 30:8, Rachel named him saying, "I have struggled with my sister and have prevailed." This name reflects the tensions between Jacob's wives and marks the warrior identity of the tribe throughout Israel's history.
H5321H.emploi: Naphtali appears in the Old Testament as one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Its descendants participate in the great collective endeavors of the people: the conquest of the land, the judgeship of Deborah and Barak (Judges 4:6), and the kingdoms of David and Solomon. The tribe is characterized by its warrior strength and rapid mobilization. The territory of Naphtali, rich and strategically located in the north, would be one of the first regions conquered by Assyria in 722 B.C.
H5321H.portee: The story of Naphtali reminds the Christian reader that God honors struggle and perseverance, and that He includes everyone in His plan, even amidst family rivalries. The faithfulness of this tribe to God's calls, particularly their response to Deborah, shows how God mobilizes His people when it comes to defending His justice.

sens: The flower of a plant, which precedes the fruit
Figuratively, that which is beautiful, delicate, or ephemeral
H5322A.detail:
1. The word refers to the flower in the botanical sense: the part of the plant that blooms before producing fruit. In the dream of Pharaoh's cupbearer reported in Genesis 40:10, the vine has three branches that "blossom" (develop their flowers) before the clusters ripen into grapes — this is the natural order of growth.
2. Figuratively, this term evokes beauty, freshness, or the brevity of what is young and delicate, like the flower that blooms before wilting.
H5322A.origine: The Hebrew word nèts comes from a root expressing the idea of budding, blooming, or germinating. It primarily denotes the act of flowering, then the flower itself as a visible and beautiful object. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, always referring to the natural image of the plant opening to the light.
H5322A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: Genesis 40:10, in the account of the symbolic dream of Pharaoh's baker. This dream predicts, through the image of the vine that blooms and produces ripe grapes, the baker's imminent restoration to his service. The usage is concrete and descriptive: flowers are the natural stage between the growth of the branch and the ripening of the fruit.
H5322A.portee: The flower reminds the believer that life follows an order created by God: growth, beauty, then fruitfulness. It invites admiration for the delicacy of the divine work and recognition, as in this dream, that God guides all things toward their fulfillment.

sens: Bird of prey with gray and white plumage, short and rounded wings, excellent hunter
Bird considered unclean according to Mosaic law
Image of speed and hunting instinct
H5322B.detail:
1. The hawk is a medium-sized bird of prey, characterized by its short, rounded wings that allow it to maneuver agilely in closed or wooded spaces to capture its prey in flight. The word specifically designates this raptor, distinct from the falcon or eagle.
2. In the law given to Israel, the hawk is listed among the birds declared unclean and forbidden for consumption (Leviticus 11:16, Deuteronomy 14:15): its status as a predatory carnivore renders it ritually unclean, like all birds of prey.
3. In Job 39:29, the hawk is presented as a model of natural instinct and wisdom inscribed in creation: its ability to take flight and orient its flight according to the seasons manifests the intelligence that God has placed in it, which man cannot teach.
H5322B.origine: The Hebrew word nets comes from the root meaning "to fly" or "to rush," which precisely evokes the characteristic behavior of this bird: its rapid flight and lightning attack. It is a concrete word that designates the animal by its most recognizable action.
H5322B.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in significant contexts. Two occurrences are found in the lists of ritual purity in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, where it symbolizes the impurity associated with the status of a predatory carnivore. The third occurrence, in God's final discourse to Job, presents the hawk as a creature whose instincts and abilities reflect divine wisdom: God challenges Job by asking if it is by human intelligence that the hawk performs its feats, suggesting that nature possesses an intelligence that God has placed in it and that man must recognize.
H5322B.portee: The hawk in the Bible teaches us to recognize the wisdom of God inscribed in creation: each creature possesses the intelligence and instincts it needs to live according to its nature. In the face of our limitations and questions about the meaning of life, Job invites us to contemplate how God provides for each creature, even the humblest, with a wisdom that we cannot teach but can only admire.

sens: To soar into the air by flapping wings
To rush or escape quickly, taking something with it
H5323.detail: 1. The literal meaning of the word describes the action of flying: a bird or winged being rises and traverses space by flapping its wings. This is the characteristic movement of creatures equipped with wings to escape, flee, or move quickly. 2. The Bible uses this verb figuratively to express a rapid and vigorous escape. In Jeremiah 48:9, the prophet calls for giving wings to Moab so that it may flee: this is a poetic image comparing the flight of the land to the speed of a bird taking off. This image emphasizes urgency and haste, as if Moab must disappear as quickly as a bird flies away.
H5323.origine: The Hebrew word נָצָא (natsa) is related to verbs of rapid movement. The basic image is that of birds flying: a sudden elevation and movement through space. This root is infrequent in biblical Hebrew, but it always expresses the idea of speed and lightness of movement, as if crossing space without obstacle.
H5323.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 48:9, where it is used figuratively. The prophet Jeremiah announces the fall of Moab, and he ironically calls for giving wings to the land so that it may fly away, like a bird fleeing danger. This poetic expression underscores both the urgency of the escape and the unreality of salvation: Moab cannot truly fly away; it can only collapse. The oracular context reinforces the dramatic and hyperbolic nature of the image.
H5323.portee: This image of rapid flight reminds the reader that in the face of divine judgment, human escape is both urgent and futile. Even if Moab had wings to flee as fast as a bird, it would not suffice to escape God's word. For the believer, this passage invites us not to place our trust in natural or human means of escape, but to recognize that only God remains sovereign over history.

sens: To be in a vertical position, standing on one's feet
To take a position in a place, to place oneself, to stop
To remain, to stay, to persist in a situation
To be established, appointed, named to a function
To rise up, to erect (referring to a building or monument)
To be firm, stable, to resist
H5324.detail:
1. To be in a vertical position, standing on one's feet: the most literal sense of the word — to stand, to be in an upright posture rather than lying down or sitting. In Genesis 18:2, three men are standing near Abraham, who ran to meet them. This contrasts with being lying down or sitting.

2. To take a position in a place, to place oneself, to stop: to go and position oneself somewhere to stay for a moment or for a specific action. In Exodus 7:15, Moses must present himself before Pharaoh at the riverbank — this involves taking a position in a given place for an important meeting.

3. To remain, to stay, to persist in a situation: to maintain one's presence or state without moving, like a sentinel or someone who is waiting. Numbers 23:6: Balak stood near his burnt offering, waiting for the result of the sacrifice.

4. To be established, appointed, named to a function: to have a role or charge assigned, to be put in place for a responsibility. In 1 Kings 9:23, the overseers appointed by Solomon are those he established to supervise the workers — they are established in authority.

5. To rise up, to erect (referring to a building or monument): to build and set up something solid and visible. In 1 Samuel 15:12, Saul erected a monument for himself, a structure raised to commemorate his victory.

6. To be firm, stable, to resist: to endure, to persist without being shaken, to hold firm. In Psalms 82:1, God stands in the assembly of God, established and immovable among His people to judge.
H5324.origine: The Hebrew root natsab fundamentally means to take one's place vertically. It evokes the image of a person standing up — a movement from low to high. The word belongs to a family of terms related to standing, establishing, and positioning. In Exodus 15:8, the waters natsab (stand up as a wall), and in Amos 7:7, the Lord stands (natsab) on a wall — the recurring image is that of something solid, erected, that does not move.
H5324.emploi: The word appears 75 times in biblical Hebrew, primarily in historical narratives and psalms. It first describes the physical position of people: Abraham sees three men standing, Moses must present himself before Pharaoh. It then extends to the appointment of officials: the stewards and overseers appointed by kings to supervise work. Finally, it takes on a theological significance: God stands in the assembly (Psalms 82:1) or stands on the wall to judge (Amos 7:7). The meaning nuances according to the context — from the literal (to stand) to the administrative (to be appointed) and the spiritual (to be established).
H5324.portee: This word invites the reader to perceive the believer's position before God: to stand before Him is to be in His presence, attentive and ready for action. It also reminds us that God Himself is established, firm, stable — a solid point of support in a changing world. Finally, for one who receives a charge, to be appointed or assigned to a function is a divine establishment, a place assigned that God entrusts.

sens: the part of a weapon held in the hand
the non-cutting part of a sword or dagger
H5325.detail:
1. The handle is the part of a bladed weapon (sword, dagger, knife) that the fighter grips with the hand to wield and direct it. It is the extension of the hilt, the place where the fingers rest.
2. In contrast to the sharp blade, the handle is the harmless area of the weapon. In Judges 3:22, during the assassination of King Eglon by Ehud, the text notes that "the handle itself went in after the blade": the blow was so violent that the hand plunged into the victim's belly was engulfed, showing how deeply the weapon penetrated.
H5325.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "that which is firmly held" or "that which remains in place." The handle is literally what one keeps a firm grip on to control the weapon. In the Greek Old Testament, this Hebrew word is rendered by terms designating the part that is grasped.
H5325.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 3:22, in the brutal and precise account of the assassination of King Eglon by the Benjamite Ehud. This warrior narrative uses this detail to show the extreme violence of the blow: the handle itself disappeared into the body of the king.
H5325.portee: This passage reminds us that the Bible does not hide the raw realities of the history of wars and God's judgments. It describes without reservation, and this detail about the engulfed handle underscores the power of the judgment executed against an enemy of Israel.

sens: solidness, firmness
power, vigor
stability, resistance
H5326.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical solidity, the firmness of a material — the idea that something holds firm, does not yield. In Daniel 2:41, it speaks of "the strength of iron" mixed with the potter's clay: iron retains its hardness, its ability not to break, while clay is fragile.
2. By extension, it refers to power, vigor — strength as the capacity to act, to hold, to resist. It is less about brute muscular strength than about robustness, endurance.
3. The word also evokes stability, that which remains unshaken. In the same verse, the empire symbolized by this mixture of iron and clay will have "something of the strength of iron": a certain solidity despite its weaknesses.
H5326.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to stand, to firm up." It expresses the idea of stability and firmness — something that stands, that does not collapse. It is the image of a posture, of a stance.
H5326.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 2:41. It is a term from the vocabulary of visions and dream interpretation: it describes a quality of the metal in the prophetic image of the statue. Daniel uses this language to explain to Nebuchadnezzar the significance of each part of the dream.
H5326.portee: This word teaches us that true strength is a matter of firmness and inner stability, not just pure power. It also reminds us that human empires, regardless of their strong elements, remain fragile and divided — an image that invites the believer to seek his strength not in the powers of the world, but in the one who remains unshaken.

sens: To enter into a verbal or physical conflict with someone
To contest authority, to rebel against a leader or God
To engage in a struggle, a dispute
To fight or argue among oneself
H5327A.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of direct conflict between two people: a dispute that can be verbal or lead to blows. In Exodus 2:13, two Hebrews "were quarreling"; in Leviticus 24:10, a young man "quarreled" with an Israelite in the camp — situations where people are in disagreement and confrontation.
2. The word can describe a more serious revolt: an open opposition to established authority. Numbers 26:9 speaks of Dathan and Abiram who "rose up" against Moses and Aaron and "rebelled" against the Lord — this is a collective act of disobedience directed against leaders and against God Himself.
3. The context of marital or family disputes shows the word applied to conflicts among close relations: two men "quarrel" in the fields (2 Samuel 14:6), or a woman intervenes when her husband "quarrels" with someone (Deuteronomy 25:11) — the idea is one of a struggle where people lose control.
H5327A.origine: The Hebrew root נצה (natsah) expresses the idea of struggle and conflict. It describes a movement of opposition, hence the translation as "quarrel" or "revolt." The word belongs to the family of terms describing direct and visible conflict between people, without the idea of simple hidden disagreement: it is an externalized confrontation.
H5327A.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Pentateuch (the first five books). It is used in two main contexts: first, ordinary disputes between two people (Exodus 2:13; 21:22; Leviticus 24:10; Deuteronomy 25:11; 2 Samuel 14:6) — the word describes a conflict that can have legal or serious consequences. Secondly, it qualifies rebellion against divine authority or that of Moses (Numbers 26:9 with Dathan and Abiram), where the conflict becomes political and religious. In all cases, it is a manifest and public conflict.
H5327A.portee: This word reminds the reader that interpersonal conflicts are not private matters without consequence: the Bible addresses them, establishes rules, and takes a stand. It also highlights the danger of organized rebellion against God and His representatives — which does not go unnoticed. For the believer, it is a lesson on the seriousness of quarrels and the importance of peace, as well as the impossibility of rebelling against God without consequences.

sens: State of destruction of a city or a building reduced to nothing
Debris, pile of stones after destruction
State of devastation of an entire region
H5327B.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the final state of a city or fortification completely destroyed: collapsed walls, razed buildings. It is the visible result of destruction, what is seen on the ground. In 2 Kings 19:25 and Isaiah 37:26, the king of Assyria has reduced "strong cities to heaps of ruins" — the image is that of piles of rubble where walls and homes once stood. 2. The word can also refer to the action of reducing to ruins, the process of destruction itself. This meaning is found in Jeremiah 4:7, where the cities "will be ruined": they will undergo destruction and become debris. 3. More broadly, the word applies to the devastation of an entire region, when war or divine judgment ravages the land and leaves a landscape of destruction and desolation.
H5327B.origine: The Hebrew root naṣah describes the process of destruction and demolition. It evokes the idea of removing, stripping away, reducing to nothing. The ruins it denotes are not merely passive debris: they are the result of a voluntary act of destruction, whether human (the Assyrian war) or divine (judgment).
H5327B.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, only in contexts of military destruction and judgment. The first two occurrences (2 Kings 19:25 and Isaiah 37:26) report the same event: the blasphemy of the king of Assyria boasting of having reduced strong cities "to heaps of ruins." The third (Jeremiah 4:7) belongs to the prophecy of judgment: the prophet announces that the cities of Judah "will be ruined" by the enemy coming from the north. In all cases, the word refers to destructions that come from a hostile power, either human or divine.
H5327B.portee: This word reminds the believer of the reality of God's judgment and the consequences of rebellion. It shows that the refusal to obey God leads to desolation and loss. But it also invites one to see how God controls events: even empires that consider themselves all-powerful ultimately execute God's plan. It is a call to repentance and a warning about the cost of pride.

sens: The flower of a plant, its initial development before the fruit
The moment when the flower transforms into ripening fruit
H5328.detail:
1. The flower is the delicate part of the plant that appears before the fruit: it is the initial stage of fruiting. In Job 15:33, the prophet describes an olive tree whose flowers have fallen — the image of an early loss, when everything is just beginning, showing how fragile and precious the flower is.
2. Metaphorically, "flower" also refers to the process of maturation, when the flower transforms and becomes ripe fruit. In Isaiah 18:5, "when the flower becomes a grape that ripens" speaks of this transition: the flower is not the final stage, but the one where true fruiting begins. It is an image of development and fulfillment.
H5328.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of blooming or flourishing. It belongs to the family of words related to growth and plant life. In nature, the flower is a symbol of fragile beauty and potential — it promises the forthcoming fruit, but it is also vulnerable to the elements and damage.
H5328.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first occurrence, in Job 15:33, uses it to evoke destruction: the flowers fall, a sign of misfortune and loss. The second, in Isaiah 18:5, employs it in a prophetic vision of divine judgment on a nation: the flower represents an early stage, and the transition to ripe fruit announces God's final action. In both cases, the word fits into an imagery of natural cycle — growth, maturation, judgment.
H5328.portee: This word reminds the reader that life, whether spiritual or material, has stages: the flower is never the end, but always a promise. It is also fragile — it can fall. For the believer, this speaks to the provisional nature of visible things and the importance of bearing fruit, not just "flowering" or appearing beautiful. The flower invites vigilance: the fruit is not yet visible, but the direction of development can be discerned.

sens: One who leads the singing in worship
One who supervises or directs a work
That which endures, that which is eternal
H5329.detail:
1. The chief musician is the musician who leads the singers and instruments of the temple. It is a role of cultic responsibility: he ensures the correct execution of the songs and their harmony with the instruments. In 1 Chronicles 15:21, Matthithia and others "lead" the song, meaning they direct and animate it for the entire assembly.
2. More broadly, the word designates one who supervises or presides over an activity: a foreman, a leader. In 2 Chronicles 2:2 and 34:12, it refers to masters of work who oversee the construction of the temple.
3. In a more abstract or poetic sense, the word can evoke what is durable, brilliant, that which perpetuates — like the voice of the chief musician who "leads" the assembly in praise that rises to the Lord.
H5329.origine: The Hebrew verb נָצַח (natsakh) expresses the idea of standing out, shining, or distinguishing oneself. Its primary meaning is "to be preeminent, to surpass." Applied to worship, it has specialized in the role of one who excels in leading, who visibly directs. In close Aramaic, the word has the same force: "to distinguish oneself" — the one who presides stands out by his function.
H5329.emploi: The word appears about 65 times in the Old Testament. Its dominant usage is musical and cultic: it appears at the head of 55 psalms ("To the chief musician"), where it designates the music director responsible for their public execution. The word also applies to foremen (2 Chronicles 2:2, 34:12) and supervisors (Ezra 3:8-9). In 1 Chronicles 23:4, the Levites are organized under chiefs. In all cases, it is a position of recognized direction or leadership.
H5329.portee: This word reminds the reader that worship, praise, and work in service to God require organization, direction, and excellence. The chief musician is not a mere executor: he is a leader who ensures that the community praises God with order and beauty. For the Christian, this suggests that serving God requires seriousness, faithfulness, and excellence, under appropriate authority.

sens: To excel, to be superior to others in quality or ability
To distinguish oneself by merits or accomplishments
H5330.detail:
1. To surpass means to exceed others in excellence, to have qualities or skills that make you better than them. It is the idea of recognized superiority. Daniel surpassed the governors and satraps of the kingdom of Persia because a superior spirit was in him (Daniel 6:3): he showed himself more capable, wiser, and more trustworthy than those around him.
2. The word also carries the idea of distinguishing oneself, rising above the crowd through personal merits. This is why the king considered establishing Daniel over the entire kingdom — he had noticed him, he had seen him excel where others remained ordinary.
H5330.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (נָצַח) that meant "to lead" or "to direct." In Aramaic, the form used here (Ithpael, a form that marks the intense or reflexive action of the verb) takes on the meaning of "to excel" or "to distinguish oneself." The root evokes the idea of one who leads, who is ahead, who surpasses: one who excels.
H5330.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 6:3, regarding Daniel in exile in Babylon. The context is one of political rivalry: the other governors and satraps, jealous, sought to find a flaw in Daniel to accuse him before the king, but Daniel surpassed them by his integrity, wisdom, and dedication. His moral and administrative excellence clearly distinguished him from the other officials of the kingdom. It was this superiority that provoked envy and ultimately put Daniel in danger, as his rivals had to invent an accusation based on his religious faith.
H5330.portee: This word reminds us that excellence comes from integrity and wisdom, not from cunning or corruption. Daniel surpassed others because a superior spirit was in him: it is a call for Christians to seek excellence in their work and life, based on their faith and righteousness, knowing that God notices and honors those who strive to please Him in the small things.

sens: Endless duration, eternity
Continuity without interruption in time
Permanence of a situation or state
Force, solidity that persists
Victory or lasting superiority
H5331.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes eternity or that which has no end: "It will never be inhabited again" (Isaiah 13:20) evokes a situation that will not change, that will last indefinitely. It is the total absence of a term.
2. It also expresses continuity: a thing that persists "without ceasing" or "continually," like Job's suffering that does not stop (Jeremiah 15:18). The idea is one of constant repetition over time.
3. Sometimes it emphasizes the permanence of a state or condition: God remains forever the refuge of His own (Psalms 9:7), or the wicked perish forever (Psalms 49:20).
4. The word can also express "force" or enduring power: "He who is the strength of Israel" (1 Samuel 15:29) denotes God's unshakeable power.
5. It sometimes carries the sense of victory or superiority that remains: the one who triumphs wins definitively.
H5331.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of shining, enduring, maintaining: the basic image is that of what persists, that does not wear out. In the Greek Old Testament, it is often rendered by words meaning "eternity" or "forever." It is a fundamental term for expressing what escapes time.
H5331.emploi: The word appears 42 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, Job, and the prophets. It is always used to speak of what does not end: God's duration, the eternity of punishment or happiness, the permanence of a promise or a threat. Sometimes translated "always" when it refers to a repeated action ("the oppressor will outrage without ceasing"), sometimes "never" in the negative ("will never be inhabited again"), and rarely "force" or "victory" when the context speaks of power (1 Samuel 15:29). The main meaning remains endless duration.
H5331.portee: This word reminds us that God exists outside of time, that His promises are unshakeable, and that His judgments are definitive. For the believer, it invites us to entrust our fears to the One who endures forever, and to take seriously the warnings of an eternal consequence of sin. It is a word that broadens our horizon beyond the present moment.

sens: The juice that flows from grapes in the press
The blood that gushes from a crushed or wounded body
The price of carnage, the bloody result of violence
H5332.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the juice that flows from grapes being pressed — a vital liquid that flows and stains. 2. By extension, it is the blood that gushes when men are crushed under fury: the text shows this literally in Isaiah 63:3, where blood has splattered on the garments of the one who treads the peoples. 3. The word also evokes the terrible consequence of divine violence: in Isaiah 63:6, the blood shed on the earth is the visible and irreversible trace of judgment.
H5332.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to flow" or "to run out," hence the image of the liquid that gushes. In Hebrew, it is very close to other words designating what flows and stains — juice, wine, blood. In the ancient Greek Bible, this Hebrew word can be rendered by terms meaning "haimai" (blood), which shows that both languages see the same link between vital juice and spilled blood.
H5332.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Isaiah 63, a passage where God speaks of His judgment on the nations. The prophet describes God entering alone into the press of His wrath: it is an image of extreme violence where peoples are crushed like grapes. The "blood" that gushes and stains the Lord's garments, which is shed on the earth, is the visible and horrifying result of this judgment. This rare and brutal word intensifies the image of carnage.
H5332.portee: This passage shows that God judges sin with real and terrible anger. The spilled blood is not a trivial metaphor: it is the expression of the ultimate cost of sin and divine justice. For the Christian, this also sheds light on why the blood of Christ on the cross has infinite value — it is the true "blood" shed for redemption, where Isaiah 63 shows the blood shed in judgment.

sens: Military post established in a city or occupied region
Soldier or troop stationed permanently to guard a place
Monument or fixed object marking a location
Person established in a position of control or authority
H5333.detail:
1. A garrison is primarily a military post established in an enemy or conquered city to control it and prevent rebellion. When David defeats the Arameans of Damascus, he places "garrisons" there to ensure his control: these are units stationed on site (2 Samuel 8:6).
2. The term also refers to the soldiers themselves, the troop occupying this post. After Jonathan struck a "garrison" of the Philistines at Geba, the Philistines learn of it, and the whole region becomes concerned (1 Samuel 13:3-4).
3. By extension, a garrison can be a fortified position, a military stronghold: Saul knew there was a Philistine post at Gibeah of God (1 Samuel 10:5).
4. The word can also refer to a stationary and durable object: Lot's wife, frozen by divine judgment, becomes a "pillar" of salt, like a frozen monument on site (Genesis 19:26).
H5333.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to place," "to establish," or "to set up." It originally designates something that is put in place, set down, hence the image of the soldier on duty, the erected object, the fixed monument. In the Old Testament, this word primarily appears in military contexts to describe the occupation of a territory by a dominant power.
H5333.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Samuel and Chronicles, as well as in 1 Kings. It is regularly used for the troops and posts that David establishes in the conquered territories (Syria, Edom), showing how he consolidates his empire. It is also found during the time of young Saul, when the Philistines still occupy Israel with military posts. Only once (Genesis 19:26), it describes Lot's wife turned into a pillar of salt, a more fixed and concrete sense. The context changes with the books: during the time of the judges and the early monarchy, the Philistine garrisons represent a threat; under David, they become tools of victory and empire.
H5333.portee: This word reminds us that military domination requires a lasting and organized presence. For the believer, it illustrates how God establishes His authority and order — not through brute force, but through attentive presence. The image of Lot's wife, frozen into a pillar, warns that divine judgment freezes those who turn away; it remains a call not to look back, but toward the promise.

sens: City of Judah in the Lowlands, near the Philistine border
H5334.detail: Netsib is a small city mentioned only once in the Bible, listed among the cities of the tribe of Judah. It was located in the Lowlands (the Shephelah), this region of hills between the Judean mountain and the Mediterranean coast, near Philistine lands. The context in Joshua 15 shows that it was part of the territory allotted to Judah during the conquest of Canaan.
H5334.origine: The Hebrew name נְצִיב (netsiv) comes from the root נצב which means "to stand" or "to be established." The word first evokes a column or pillar — something solid and unchanging. By extension, it designates a fortified place or a garrison, as a garrison represents an established and permanent presence. The name of this city likely reflects its strategic role as a outpost in the border region.
H5334.emploi: Netsib appears only once in the usages provided by the Bible: in Joshua 15:43. It is cited in the list of cities allocated to the tribe of Judah during the division of the land of Canaan. This enumeration, in chapter 15 of the book of Joshua, is part of the description of the territory that Judah received as an inheritance. Although very little documented in the biblical text, its location in the Lowlands, a region of contact and tension between Judah and Philistia, suggests that it had strategic importance for the defense of the Judean territory.

sens: Leader of a family of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H5335.detail: Netsiach is the name of a man who lived during the time of exile and the return to Jerusalem. He was the head of a family of servants attached to the temple service, and he led this family during the return from exile in Babylon under the leadership of Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:54). His name also appears in the similar list in Nehemiah 7:56, confirming that the descendants of Netsiach were part of these workers of the restored temple.
H5335.origine: The name Netsiach comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be eminent" or "to be distinguished" — hence its meaning: "preeminent" or "one who dominates." It was a name that expressed a form of dignity or preeminence, appropriate for a family leader.
H5335.emploi: Netsiach is mentioned twice in the Bible, in parallel contexts: first in the book of Ezra (2:54), and then in the book of Nehemiah (7:56). These two passages list the families of temple servants who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel, around 538 BC. The "sons of Netsiach" form one of these families. The repetition in these two books, which complete the story of the return from exile, shows the documentary importance of this genealogy for the restored people of Israel. Netsiach and his family represent these essential temple workers, whose service helped to rebuild the worship in Jerusalem.

sens: To forcibly pull something or someone away, to rescue from someone else
To save a person from danger, death, an enemy, or suffering
To protect, to secure
To strip away, remove, confiscate property
To deliver from sin, guilt, moral evil
H5337.detail:
1. To forcibly pull away: the word evokes the image of taking something from someone else's hands, even against resistance. When Jacob says, "God has taken away the wealth of our father," it refers to confiscated or removed property (Genesis 31:16). It also means to strip someone of their possessions.
2. To save from danger: this means to rescue a person from immediate peril, from an enemy, from death. The Psalmist asks God to deliver him "from those who plunder him" (Psalms 35:10), and Jeremiah receives the promise that the Lord will deliver him from his enemies (Jeremiah 15:20).
3. To protect and secure: this includes the idea of preserving someone from ongoing danger, like a shepherd who pulls a sheep from the jaws of a lion.
4. To strip away property: this means to take away, confiscate, dispossess. During the Exodus from Egypt, God took away the riches of the Egyptians that the Hebrews took (Exodus 12:36).
5. To deliver morally and spiritually: beyond physical danger, the word can refer to liberation from sin and guilt, the saving action of God that redeems His people from all oppression of evil.
H5337.origine: The Hebrew verb נָצַל comes from a root that means "to pull out," "to tear away," "to remove." It expresses the idea of a violent yet beneficial gesture: pulling something or someone toward oneself, away from danger or from another hand. The root also appears in the name נְצִילִים ("rescued ones") and in various verbal forms that all retain this nuance of extraction or rescue. It is a concrete word whose meaning easily transposes from the physical realm to the spiritual realm.
H5337.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible (nearly 200 occurrences): it is found in historical narratives, psalms, prophets, and wisdom poems. It is used in very varied contexts: literally, to pull away from plunder or property (Genesis 31:16, Exodus 12:36), to save from war or slavery (1 Samuel 4:8, Exodus 6:6), or to protect from a malicious individual (Psalms 35:10). Often, it is God who delivers His people: from Egypt, from enemies, from illness, from peril. The word also applies to the personal salvation of the believer in the face of evil. In all these cases, the central idea remains that of an intervention that pulls one out of a bad situation.
H5337.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is not passive in the face of evil and suffering: He intervenes, He pulls away, He saves. It is a word of hope for those who are going through trials or oppression. It also invites us to recognize that all freedom, all salvation comes from the powerful hand of God, not from our own strength. The verb teaches that deliverance is one of God's great works toward His people.

sens: To pull someone from danger, from a perilous situation
To deliver someone from oppression or hostile authority
To exercise divine power of protection and salvation
H5338.detail:
1. The verb primarily expresses the concrete action of pulling someone from peril: removing someone from a situation that threatens their life or integrity. In Daniel 6:14, the king strives to "save" Daniel by pulling him from the lion's den—he actively seeks to rescue him from the danger that awaits.
2. More broadly, it means to deliver someone from the domination of an enemy or oppression. It is an extraction from a hostile power. Daniel 6:27 affirms that the God of Israel "saves" His people, meaning He pulls them from the hand of their adversaries and from any threat against them.
3. Finally, when used for God, the word takes on a spiritual and cosmic significance: it denotes the unique divine power to save, which no other god possesses (Daniel 3:29). It is an assertion of sovereignty: only the true God can truly protect and preserve.
H5338.origine: This Aramaic word is the counterpart of the Hebrew verb נָצַל (natzal, H5337), which literally means "to pull out" or "to draw out." The root expresses the idea of movement: to extract something or someone from a place or situation. The Aramaic form retains this fundamental meaning and is regularly used to describe the divine act of deliverance in the narratives of the Book of Daniel, where the people of Israel are grappling with foreign powers.
H5338.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Book of Daniel, always in contexts of mortal danger and miraculous deliverance. It is first used regarding the power of pagan gods (Daniel 3:29)—a negative assertion: no god can save like the God of Israel. It then applies to the king's intention (Daniel 6:14) to save Daniel by human means. Finally, it characterizes the divine action itself (Daniel 6:27), by which God delivered Daniel from the power of the lions. In all cases, the word emphasizes an extraction from immediate and grave peril.
H5338.portee: This word reveals the believer's trust in God's unique ability to protect him in the face of earthly threats and hostile powers. It affirms that salvation is not primarily an abstract moral matter, but a concrete act: God acts to pull His people from danger. This certainty encourages the Christian to entrust themselves to God in trials, knowing that God alone possesses the true power of deliverance.

sens: Flower of a plant or tree, at the moment it blooms.
Figuratively: delicate and ephemeral beauty.
H5339.detail:
1. The word designates the flower at the moment of its blooming, this colorful and fragrant part of the plant that attracts attention and heralds life. In the Song of Solomon, "the flowers appear on the earth" marks the return of spring and fertility: it is the image of renewal and joy after winter (Song of Solomon 2:12).
2. The flower also evokes all that is beautiful yet fragile, what shines and charms but lasts little. It symbolizes delicate beauty, the ephemeral splendor of what passes quickly—a beauty that is looked upon with tenderness precisely because it does not last.
H5339.origine: The Hebrew word nitssan comes from a root that means "to emerge," "to come out"—the image of the flower that springs from the ground and blooms. It is related to terms that denote flowering and youth. It is a concrete and vivid name, rooted in simple observation of nature.
H5339.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Solomon (2:12). This poetic context celebrates the beauty of spring and love: the flowers symbolize the moment when all creation awakens and breathes. It is a word reserved for poetry and lyrical expression, never for ordinary language.
H5339.portee: The flower reminds us that beauty exists in creation and is good to behold. It also invites us to see that all that shines and charms on earth has a fragility—a truth that can help us place our hearts elsewhere than on what passes. At the same time, celebrating the flowers of spring is to recognize with the Song of Solomon that joy, renewal, and tenderness between loved ones are gifts from God to cherish.

sens: To shine with a bright and intermittent light, like a twinkling light
To shine brightly, referring to a polished surface or a shiny metal
H5340.detail:
1. To sparkle means to shine with a bright light that seems to tremble or dance, like sparks. In Ezekiel 1:7, the feet of the heavenly creatures "sparkled like polished bronze": this is the image of a smooth, shiny metallic surface that reflects light with intensity and regularity.
2. The word also describes the radiant and luminous shine of something that glows, especially when it is polished or shiny. This brightness can be alarming or majestic, conveying the holiness and power of what appears — here, the wonderful creatures that the prophet Ezekiel contemplates in his vision.
H5340.origine: The Hebrew verb נָצַץ (natsats) comes from a root that expresses the idea of brightness and brilliance. The word evokes the concrete image of light that bursts forth or dances on a surface. It belongs to the family of verbs related to luminous appearance in Hebrew, alongside words that express splendor and clarity.
H5340.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the grand vision of Ezekiel in chapter 1. The prophet describes the heavenly creatures surrounding God's throne, and he chooses this rare and expressive word to account for the supernatural brilliance of their feet. This unique usage emphasizes the extraordinary, the unexpected: it is not an ordinary detail, but a trait of splendor that marks the theophany — the appearance of God in His majesty.
H5340.portee: When Ezekiel sees the heavenly creatures sparkle like polished bronze, he contemplates the visible manifestation of God's holiness. For the reader, this word reminds us that the divine presence is accompanied by unimaginable beauty and clarity, inspiring both fear and wonder. It is an invitation to recognize the greatness of Him who reveals Himself through these luminous images.

sens: To watch over someone or something, to ensure its safety
To preserve from danger, to protect
To observe a law, a commandment, a word faithfully
To retain in one's heart or memory
To keep secret, to hold to oneself
To serve as a sentinel, to guard
H5341.detail:
1. To keep primarily means to actively watch over: to look at, to keep an eye on someone or something to prevent it from escaping or being damaged. This is the task of a guardian or sentinel. In Jeremiah 4:16, it is shouted, "Watchmen, come!" to call those who watch over the cities.
2. To protect goes further: it means to keep someone safe by defending them against evil or danger. Psalm 25:21 asks God that innocence and uprightness "protect" the one who hopes in Him, like armor.
3. To observe or keep a law means to live in accordance with it, to respect it faithfully. Proverbs 28:7 praises "the one who keeps the law," who makes it their rule of life. Psalm 119:33 asks God to teach His way "so that I may keep it to the end."
4. To retain in one's heart or memory means to memorize, not to forget. Proverbs 4:23 says, "Keep your heart more than anything else," meaning pay attention to what is happening within you.
5. To keep secret means not to disclose, to silence. Proverbs 7:10 says that this woman had "craftiness in her heart," hidden, which she kept.
6. The participle refers to one who keeps watch, the sentinel or guardian responsible for surveillance: an active and ongoing role.
H5341.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "watching" or "being vigilant." The Hebrew word is related to terms meaning protection and vigilance. In the Greek of the New Testament, this verb from the Old Testament is often rendered as "phulassô" (to keep, to protect), which shares the same image: that of active vigilance and defense. The root fundamentally expresses sustained and responsible attention.
H5341.emploi: This verb appears 62 times in the provided biblical usages, especially in the Psalms, Proverbs, and Prophets, revealing its importance in Old Testament spirituality. It primarily describes God's action: Exodus 34:7 says that God "keeps" His love to a thousand generations. The Psalms often place it in the mouth of the believer who asks God to "keep" his life (Psalm 31:24) or who commits to "keep" His commandments (Psalm 119:2). In Proverbs, it designates the wisdom that "protects" and "keeps" those who seek it (Proverbs 2:8; 4:6). Isaiah uses it to speak of the vine that the Lord "will keep" or the righteous that He "will protect" (Isaiah 27:3; 42:6). The meaning shifts from the concrete (watching over a city, Jeremiah 4:16) to the abstract (keeping His word, His law, one's heart).
H5341.portee: This word enriches the Christian's faith on two levels. First, it assures that God "keeps" us: not passively, but with active and devoted vigilance — a protection that lasts. Secondly, it calls the believer to "keep": to observe God's commandments, to retain His teaching in the heart, to preserve the purity of life. To keep is not a heavy burden, but an expression of love and trust towards Him who keeps us.

sens: A young shoot that arises from the roots or trunk of a tree
A descendant of a royal or dynastic lineage
A person or people that God has planted for His work
A leader or successor emerging from a princely line
H5342.detail:
1. A shoot is primarily a living plant sprout that emerges from the wood or roots of a tree. It is the young, fragile branch full of life that develops from the stump. In Isaiah 14:19, the body of a king is compared to a branch that is despised — the image of the shoot serves to illustrate the fragility and insignificance of a corpse cast aside in contempt.

2. The shoot is also used figuratively to refer to a descendant who continues a royal dynasty. In Daniel 11:7, "a shoot from his roots will arise in his place": this speaks of a successor who will emerge from the king's line, a political heir who will take the power and authority of the predecessor.

3. The shoot also represents the people that God cultivates for His own glory. In Isaiah 60:21, the Lord says: "It is the shoot that I have planted, the work of My hands" — the image of divine gardening: God plants His people like one plants a tree, so that they may grow and bear fruit for His glory.

4. Finally, it is a messianic and prophetic figure. In Isaiah 11:1, "a shoot will come up from the stump of Jesse" announces a royal descendant of David who will be born when the stump seems dead — it is a promise of divine renewal despite the appearance of ruin.
H5342.origine: The Hebrew word נֵצֶר (nétser) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "keeping" or "preserving," but its primary meaning is that of a young shoot that is preserved and cultivated. The word appears rarely in the Old Testament: it is always an image of fragile growth but imbued with spiritual significance. The family of this word includes other terms for branches and shoots, but nétser retains this particular nuance: it is the shoot that emerges with a promise of the future.
H5342.emploi: The word nétser appears four times in the Old Testament, and always in prophetic or royal contexts full of significance. In Isaiah 11:1, it announces the future Messiah who will come from the dormant lineage of David. In Isaiah 60:21, it describes the restored people that God constitutes after the exile, His project of creation and work. In Daniel 11:7, it names a dynastic successor who emerges and seizes power. In Isaiah 14:19, it represents the disdain cast upon the corpse of a king — an ironic usage where the shoot becomes an image of weakness and vanity. The word thus circulates between messianic promise, divine work of people, dynastic heritage, and the vanity of what seems great in the eyes of the world.
H5342.portee: This word teaches that God cultivates His people like divine gardening, with patience and purpose. It also proclaims hope: even when everything seems dry and dead (the stump of Jesse), God brings forth the new and the living. For the believer, it is a powerful image of personal renewal — we are called to be shoots of God, planted to bear fruit for His glory, despite our apparent fragility.

sens: Of immaculate whiteness, without stain or blemish
Without mixture of foreign elements, of uniform quality
Morally blameless, innocent
Free from any defect or imperfection
H5343.detail: 1. The word first describes a perfect whiteness or clarity, like that of wool. In Daniel's vision, the hair of the Ancient of Days is compared to 'pure' wool: an absolute and immaculate whiteness that shines. 2. It also refers to what has not been mixed or altered, preserving its essence intact — like pure gold without alloy or water without impurities. 3. Figuratively, the pure is one who has done no wrong, who is morally clean, innocent of guilt. 4. More broadly, it is what is perfect, free from any defect or stain, spiritually and materially.
H5343.origine: The Hebrew word נְקֵא (neqe) is related to a root meaning 'to clean' or 'to polish.' It denotes what has been purified or shines with cleanliness. In the Hebrew Bible, purity is a central category: ritual (what can be approached or offered at the temple), moral (what is just and guiltless), and physical (what is not defiled or sick). The word always evokes excellence and integrity.
H5343.emploi: The word נְקֵא appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in Daniel 7:9. In this major vision of the prophet, the Ancient of Days — God Himself in His terrifying and glorious manifestation — is described with 'pure' hair like wool. This purity expresses eternity, absolute holiness, and total absence of stain or decline in the one who sits on the judgment throne. The image emphasizes that God is perfectly preserved and immaculate, beyond any touch of time or evil.
H5343.portee: For the believer, this vision reminds us that the God who judges is Himself radically holy and pure. The purity of the Ancient of Days contrasts with the impurity and guilt of men and kingdoms that pass into judgment. It invites the reader to recognize the transcendence and perfection of the one who calls us to holiness and repentance.

sens: To make a hole by piercing
To mark something or someone to identify or distinguish them
To expressly name someone for a function or task
To fix, determine, or specify something
H5344A.detail:
1. The first concrete meaning: to dig or make a hole by perforating a material. This is what the priest Jehoiada does when he 'pierces' a hole in the lid of a chest to receive the money from the offerings (2 Kings 12:9). The image is of a physical action that creates an opening.

2. A natural extension: to mark someone or something by 'pricking' or 'inscribing,' in the sense of designating by name or characteristic to distinguish them among others. This is close to the first meaning, but more fixed: one 'designates' by naming explicitly.

3. The most common meaning in the Bible: to name someone expressly for a charge, responsibility, or role. Thus the heads of the Levitical families are 'designated' to distribute the portions to the priests (2 Chronicles 31:19), or eighteen thousand men of Manasseh are designated to establish King David (1 Chronicles 12:31).

4. From there, to fix or determine something precisely and definitively: when Jacob says 'set your wages for me' (Genesis 30:28), he asks the shepherd Laban to specify, to clearly decide what his price will be.
H5344A.origine: The Hebrew root קב (qav) evokes the action of pricking, marking, tracing a line. The verb נָקַב (naqav) is its intensive form: not only to trace, but to 'pierce' completely, creating a visible opening. This dual meaning — first physical (to pierce), then administrative or designative (to mark someone's name, to specify) — reflects the idea that giving a name is also to 'make a mark' that distinguishes and identifies.
H5344A.emploi: The verb נָקַב appears 17 times in the Old Testament. The meaning 'to pierce' or 'to perforate' is clearly attested in 2 Kings 12:9 (the hole in the chest) and in Job 40:19 (to pierce the nose of a creature). The meaning 'to designate' or 'to expressly name' largely dominates: it is found in administrative and priestly contexts when it comes to specifying by name who will have such a function (1 Chronicles 12:31; 2 Chronicles 31:19), or in judicial-liturgical contexts when a sin or a guilty party is 'named' explicitly (Leviticus 24:11, where the name blasphemy is 'pronounced'). The meaning 'to fix' or 'to determine' appears in Genesis 30:28 (set your wages) and Isaiah 62:2 (a new name fixed). The context always indicates the idea of a voluntary and definitive action, never of a mere intention.
H5344A.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, naming and designating are not neutral acts: they establish an identification, a charge, a responsibility. When God 'designates' someone, He marks them as His own for a mission. For the believer, it is an invitation to take seriously the name given by God and the functions to which he is called in the Church or his life.

sens: To utter insulting or contemptuous words against God
To outrage the sacred name of the Lord with words
To profane by word what is holy
H5344B.detail:
1. The Hebrew verb primarily means to say words that pierce or transfix — one can imagine a word that wounds, that offends. To blaspheme is to utter insulting or contemptuous words directly against God, against His name or nature. In Leviticus 24:16, whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord commits a crime so grave that he incurs death: the whole assembly must stone him.
2. The outrage particularly targets the name of God, His revealed identity. It is an act of rebellion that denies His honor and authority. The text emphasizes: whether foreigner or native, the law applies equally, for offending the divine name is an absolute transgression.
H5344B.origine: The Hebrew word נָקַב comes from a root meaning 'to pierce' or 'to transfix.' The image is of a word that pierces like a weapon, that wounds. This image of a sharp or destructive word is found in other biblical passages: words, like a sword, can wound deeply. Blasphemy is therefore a word that 'pierces' the honor of God.
H5344B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Pentateuch in this form, in Leviticus 24:16. It is used in the context of a capital law: blasphemy against the name of the Lord leads to stoning. This unique but solemn prohibition shows that blaspheming against God was considered one of the gravest crimes in Israelite legislation. The text repeats the verb twice ('whoever blasphemes... for having blasphemed') to emphasize its importance and unforgivable nature.
H5344B.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that words carry enormous weight: they are never neutral, especially when they concern God. The seriousness with which the Law treats blasphemy teaches that our speech must be filled with respect for the Holy Name. It is a call to vigilance over what we say and to recognize that God and His honor cannot be offended with impunity.

sens: hole, cavity or groove carved in an object
passage or channel through which something flows
element of adornment or decoration fitted into a setting
wind musical instrument with holes
H5345.detail:
1. In Hebrew, this word primarily refers to a hole, cavity, or groove: it is the hollow that is carved into stone, metal, or wood. It is a very concrete image of manual work.
2. By extension, it refers to a passage or channel: when something is pierced, a passage is created through which something can cross or escape.
3. In the work of the goldsmith or jeweler, it is the cavity where a precious stone or ornament is set into its mounting. It is a technical term of the trade.
4. Through this hole or passage, a musical sound can be produced: this is why the word comes to designate a flute or a wind instrument. In Ezekiel 28:13, the king of Tyre sees his tambourines and flutes serving his magnificence from the moment of his creation.
H5345.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to pierce" or "to dig." In the same family, there are words that speak of what is pierced, holed, or dug. The basic image is that of work: digging, making a passage, opening a void. From this comes the idea of cavity, and then that of the wind instrument, since a flute is nothing more than an object pierced with holes that produce sounds.
H5345.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 28:13, in the prophet's vision of the king of Tyre. The text describes his past splendor: he was covered with precious stones and possessed tambourines and flutes, instruments of music and luxury. The word is translated here as "flute" because in this biblical context, it is the musical instrument that is in view. The usage shows that the word, although technical and rare, is understood as an object of magnificence and wealth.
H5345.portee: This word reminds us that God is the creator of all beauty, precious objects, and musical talents. Ezekiel's vision shows us how material and artistic splendor can become an occasion for pride and downfall if turned away from God. The flute, a symbol of art and pleasure, invites the reader to honor the Creator rather than His gifts.

sens: City of the tribe of Naphtali, in Palestine
H5346.detail: Adami-Nékeb is a locality established on the border of the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of Canaan. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the account of the borders of this tribe (Joshua 19:33).
H5346.origine: The name is composed of two elements: Adami means "red" or "red earth" in Hebrew, and Nékeb means "cave" or "narrow passage." The full name likely designates a place characterized by a cave or a natural pass. The second element reflects the rugged geography of the Galilee region.
H5346.emploi: Adami-Nékeb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 19:33, in the enumeration of localities that marked the border of the territory of Naphtali. It is cited among other cities such as Heleph, Allon, Taanach, and Jabneel, all located in northern Galilee. This mention is set in the context of the division of Canaan among the twelve tribes after the conquest.

sens: Adult human female
Female child
Female animal
H5347.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to an adult woman, in contrast to a man. In Genesis 1:27, God creates "man and woman" in His image, establishing from the outset that this sexual distinction is part of His creation. This is the most common meaning in the Bible.

2. It also applies to a girl or young female. In Leviticus 27:5, the law sets different monetary values according to age: "from five to twenty years, your estimation shall be twenty shekels for a male, and ten shekels for a female." The word does not primarily designate a function or role, but simply the female sex of the one being referred to.

3. In texts about sacrifices and purity, the word also applies to female animals. In Leviticus 4:32, one can offer "a female without defect" as a sin offering, just as one can offer a male. The same anatomical distinction extends to all living creatures.
H5347.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to pierce" or "to dig," evoking the opening of the female body. This image of the piercing or cavity underlies the idea of the female sex. In Hebrew, this root also generates other words related to femininity. The word regularly appears in conjunction with "male" (זָכָר, zakhar) to express the natural order of creation and the prescriptions of the Law.
H5347.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Genesis, Leviticus, and Numbers. It systematically appears in creation narratives ("male and female"), in lists of animals taken on the Ark ("male and female"), and in the purity codes and sacrifices of Leviticus, where it designates both the ritual victim and the woman in cases of impurity. In Jeremiah 31:22, the prophet announces that "the woman surrounds the male," a unique image of inversion or eschatological renewal. Everywhere, the word expresses an anatomical and biological fact, rarely a moral or spiritual status.
H5347.portee: This word reminds us that man and woman are created together and equally before God, bearing His image without distinction (Genesis 1:27). In the Law, the use of this word shows that women are not excluded from the prescriptions of purity, sacrifice, and religious life: they are fully subjects of divine revelation. It is a soberly inclusive word that anchors the place of women in God's design from the beginning.

sens: Marked with spots or points of different colors
(Referring to animals) Having white or colored markings on the coat
H5348.detail:
1. The word literally designates something that bears spots or points, distinct marks scattered over a surface. In the story of Jacob and Laban (Genesis 30), it qualifies the sheep and goats that are not of a single color: "I will pass today through all your flock; set apart from the sheep every spotted and speckled lamb" (Genesis 30:32). These animals have areas of different colors, notably white or black spots on their fur.
2. The word regularly applies to animals that are variegated by natural generation: the sheep "came into heat near the branches, and they bore young that were striped, spotted, and speckled" (Genesis 30:39). This is an observable reality among flocks: some lambs are born with spots or stripes, while others are of a uniform color.
H5348.origine: The Hebrew word נָקֹד (naqod) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to make points" or "to prick," hence the idea of punctuated marks. The image is that of a surface dotted with distinct points or spots. The word describes the concrete visual aspect, without particular connotation: it is simply the natural or visible pattern of the coat.
H5348.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Bible, exclusively in the story of Jacob and Laban (Genesis 30-31), where it always concerns determining Jacob's wages. Jacob requests in exchange all the spotted and speckled animals, and it is on this basis that he becomes wealthy: the word specifically designates these animals recognizable by their markings. It is often used in conjunction with other terms ("striped," "speckled," "black") to describe the different visual categories of the flock. It is a strictly descriptive term, without emotional nuance.
H5348.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, even the concrete details of ordinary life — the coats of animals, the flocks — are important and observed with care. The story of Jacob shows how God can rely on visible and natural realities to accomplish His purposes. The distinctive markings of the spotted animals become the sign of work and wages: a small physical detail becomes spiritually significant in the unfolding of divine providence.

sens: one who raises and keeps flocks of sheep
one who sells or trades sheep
man who owns large herds
H5349.detail:
1. The shepherd is primarily one who raises and keeps flocks of sheep — this is the primary occupation. Amos, the prophet, is described as "one of the shepherds of Tekoa" (Amos 1:1), indicating a role of care and guardianship over the animals.
2. The word also refers to one who sells or trades sheep, or even collects the products of the flock. Mesha, king of Moab, "owned flocks" and paid tribute in lambs and rams with their wool (2 Kings 3:4) — he exploits his animals for profit.
3. More broadly, it refers to an owner of large herds, a man rich in livestock, often a chief or a king who controls these riches.
H5349.origine: The Hebrew word נֹקֵד comes from a root that fundamentally means "to pasture" or "to keep livestock." It is formed to designate the agent — one who performs the action. In Hebrew, the same type of word can apply to different roles related to sheep: to keep, to raise, or to possess in large numbers. The root evokes the image of the shepherd standing among his flock, watching over each animal.
H5349.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided Hebrew Bible, in two very different contexts that show the versatility of the term. In 2 Kings 3:4, it refers to a powerful king who possesses enormous wealth in livestock — here the word emphasizes the owner and producer. In Amos 1:1, Amos is simply "one of the shepherds of Tekoa," which rather highlights his concrete work as a guardian of flocks. The royal context of 2 Kings contrasts with the humble context of Amos, showing that the shepherd can be both a simple worker and a man of wealth.
H5349.portee: This word reminds us that the occupation of shepherd, humble in appearance, was honorable in Israel, as it allowed Amos to become a prophet. It also evokes the closeness between the shepherd and the image of the spiritual pastor that God Himself exercises toward His people — a poignant contrast: the true shepherd watches over souls with love, while the shepherd of the world accumulates wealth and tribute.

sens: fragment detached from a bread or cake
small piece of food that crumbles
hard bread or dry cake that breaks apart
H5350.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a fragment of bread or biscuit that has naturally broken off. At the gates of Jericho, the Gibeonites carry bread that has become dry and brittle, all in crumbs (Joshua 9:5), to prove that they have come from very far away.
2. More broadly, it refers to a small piece of food that crumbles easily between the fingers — the image is that of stale bread that disintegrates. Joshua 9:12 confirms this: the bread was fresh when they took it, but now it is dry and in crumbs.
3. The word can also refer to food itself in its crumbled or fragmented form, like the dry cakes brought as an offering to the prophet Elijah in 1 Kings 14:3 — compact foods that are easy to break.
H5350.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to break" or "to crumble." It is formed from a very concrete notion: something that breaks into a thousand pieces, that falls to dust. It is a word that paints the image of fragile food, worn by time or easily breakable by hand — stale bread or hardened cake.
H5350.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always related to food on a journey or as an offering. The first two uses (Joshua 9:5 and 9:12) describe the dried bread of the Gibeonites who come from afar: they want to justify their long journey by showing that their food has reduced to crumbs. The third use (1 Kings 14:3) speaks of dry cakes brought to Elijah. In all cases, the word emphasizes the fragmented, fragile, or aged nature of the food.
H5350.portee: This word reminds us that food, a sign of covenant and divine provision, can wear out and deteriorate. For the reader, it speaks to the weariness of the human journey, the fatigue of earthly roads — and invites us to seek food that does not crumble, a promise that never ages.

sens: small round and shiny ornament with a hole
drop of liquid
H5351.detail:
1. A small shiny ball, often made of precious metal, pierced in the center to be strung on a thread or cord: it is a piece of jewelry worn for its beauty. In Song of Solomon 1:11, the beloved promises his beloved "chains of gold with pearls of silver" — an image of beauty and seduction that speaks of the delicate adornment of a loved woman.
2. A drop of liquid that shines like a pearl: the image of a small sparkling sphere that can be observed on the skin or a surface.
H5351.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to pierce" or "to point" — the idea of a small pointed or pearled object that shines. The notion of "point" or "drop" is its primary image. In biblical Hebrew, this word is rare and primarily refers to the precious ornament, preferably silver worked into small pearls.
H5351.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in a lyrical poem from the Song of Solomon where the beloved tenderly describes the adornment of his friend. It is set in a context of love and luxury, where the details of physical beauty celebrate mutual attraction. Its poetic and rare use underscores the importance of the moment and the object in the intimate context of the love song.
H5351.portee: This word invites the reader to see beauty as something precious and crafted with care. In the Song of Solomon, it reminds us that human love can be expressed through concrete gestures of tenderness and adornment — it is a biblical invitation not to despise physical beauty and the small luxuries that testify to affection.
