sens: To be exempt from a consequence, penalty, or obligation
To be pure, innocent, free from guilt
To be delivered, freed, released from a situation or bond
To leave someone unpunished, to acquit them
H5352.detail:
1. To remain unpunished means to escape punishment or the consequence of a fault: it is not to suffer the deserved penalty. The false witness "will not remain unpunished" (Proverbs 19:9), the seducer "will not remain unpunished" (Proverbs 6:29). It is the idea of a debt of guilt that is paid — or not paid.
2. To be innocent or pure means to be free from guilt, without stain. The woman who has undergone the jealousy test "will be declared innocent and will have children" (Numbers 5:28): she is declared pure before God.
3. To be released or freed means to be liberated from an obligation or attachment. Abraham tells his servant: you will be "released" from the oath if the woman refuses (Genesis 24:8) — you are free from this bond.
4. To leave unpunished is a divine or human action: not to punish one who could be punished. God tells Jeremiah: "I will discipline you fairly; I cannot leave you unpunished" (Jeremiah 30:11) — even the Lord's just discipline does not leave without correction.
H5352.origine: The Hebrew root naqah (נקה) evokes the idea of being empty, cleared, clean — like a house emptied of its inhabitants. From this image of emptiness arises the meaning of purity (cleared of sin), of guilt (emptied of guilt = innocent), and of exemption (free from obligation, escaped from penalty). The word belongs to the family of terms of innocence and purity in Hebrew, dominated by the idea of cleanness and clarity.
H5352.emploi: This verb is used 33 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom and prophetic books. Three usages dominate: (1) To remain unpunished, not to escape punishment — this is the most frequent usage, particularly in Proverbs (6:29, 11:21, 19:5, 19:9) and among the prophets (Jeremiah 25:29, 30:11; Nahum 1:3). The text affirms that certain acts never remain unpunished. (2) To be innocent or pure — Numbers 5:28 speaks of the woman recognized as innocent after the test. (3) To be released or freed from an obligation — Genesis 24:8 with the oath from which one can be released. God Himself "cannot leave unpunished" (Jeremiah 30:11), reflecting His justice: He will discipline, but fairly.
H5352.portee: This word reminds us of an essential biblical truth: no act of wrongdoing escapes God's sight. Lies, covetousness, injustice "will not remain unpunished." But it also teaches that purity and innocence exist — one can be recognized as innocent before God. For the modern reader, it is a word of comfort and warning: comfort for the victims (divine justice will see), warning for the one who sins (no guilt is hidden from God).

sens: Head of a family of temple servants returning from exile
Head of a family of exiles whose genealogy was uncertain
H5353G.detail:
1. Nekoda is a personal name that designates a head of a family. He is mentioned as the leader of a branch of temple servants returning from exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:48). These temple servants formed a class of ministers serving the divine worship.
2. The same name also appears to designate a leader of another family of exiles: these came from cities like Tel Melah, Tel Harsa, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not prove their Israelite ancestry or establish their genealogy (Nehemiah 7:50). Despite this uncertainty about their origins, they also participated in the return with Zerubbabel.
H5353G.origine: The name Nekoda means "distinguished" or "remarkable" in Hebrew. It is a patronymic — the name of a person from whom entire families descend at the time of the return from exile in Babylon (around 538 B.C.). Like many Hebrew proper names, it carries a positive meaning.
H5353G.emploi: Nekoda is mentioned twice in the lists of returning exiles: first in Ezra 2:48, where he designates a head of a family of temple servants, and then in Nehemiah 7:50, in a parallel and almost identical list. These two passages come from administrative documents of the return, which enumerate the families and groups that left Babylon to rebuild Jerusalem and its temple under the leadership of Zerubbabel. The two usages concern the same families: the first focuses on the temple servants of good lineage, while the second also includes those whose origin was doubtful.

sens: Head of a family of temple servants returned from exile
Name of a family whose members could not prove their genealogy
H5353H.detail: Nekoda is a name borne by the head of a family of servants attached to the temple. This family is mentioned in the lists of those who returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, around 538 B.C. According to Ezra 2:60, the sons of Nekoda formed a group of six hundred fifty-two people. This same group is listed again in Nehemiah 7:62 with the number of six hundred forty-two members, suggesting that it is the same record consulted at two different times or with counting variations. The family of Nekoda belonged to the category of temple servants (those who assisted the priests in their ministry) and was part of the families that, despite being unable to justify their genealogy or prove their belonging to Israel, were nonetheless allowed to return and settle in Jerusalem during the reconstruction of the temple.
H5353H.origine: The name Nekoda means "distinguished" or "marked" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of standing out or being noticed. It is a personal name that became a family or clan name, as is often the case in the Bible where the head of a household gives his name to his descendants.
H5353H.emploi: Nekoda is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in texts concerning the return from exile: in Ezra 2:60 and in Nehemiah 7:62. These two passages are practically identical: they list the families of temple servants who returned with Zerubbabel. The family of Nekoda is presented alongside the families of Delajah and Tobijah, in a section that addresses those who could not prove their genealogy and their Israelite status, but who still participated in the reconstruction of the community. The exact number of descendants of Nekoda varies slightly between the two passages (652 in Ezra, 642 in Nehemiah), reflecting common variations in ancient manuscripts or counts of that time.
H5353H.portee: The name of Nekoda reminds us that the return from exile included not only pure-blooded Israelites but also all those who had attached themselves to the people of God and who desired to participate in the restoration of the temple and religious life in Jerusalem. This illustrates divine grace towards foreigners and slaves who identified with the people of God, an openness that foreshadows the welcome of all believers in Christ, regardless of their origin.

sens: To feel disgust, aversion towards something or someone
To experience deep weariness, moral fatigue in the face of life
H5354.detail: 1. This verb expresses a visceral, physical reaction: disgust, aversion. It is to reject something with repulsion, like pushing away something foul. 2. Here, in Job 10:1, the meaning expands to existential fatigue: Job is so discouraged, so weary of life that he feels disgust. It is no longer just a passing repulsion, but a deep frustration that leads to bitterness and complaint.
H5354.origine: The Hebrew root נקט suggests the idea of pushing away, rejecting forcefully. The context of Job (a book of wisdom in the face of suffering) shows that the word can refer not only to physical or moral disgust but also to that fatigue of the soul that accompanies distress.
H5354.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Job 10:1. Job, grappling with extreme suffering, declares that his soul is disgusted with life. This unique usage reveals a moment of spiritual crisis: the wise man, usually in control, expresses here a repulsion towards his fate and existence itself.
H5354.portee: This word helps the reader understand the depth of Job's suffering. It is not a passing complaint, but an existential disgust: life weighs on him to the point that he feels repulsion. This resonates with any believer who has experienced moments of despair and validates the honest expression of spiritual fatigue before God.

sens: Who has not committed the fault or crime of which he is accused
Who incurs no guilt or punishment
Freed from an obligation or commitment
Who has not shed blood
Pure before God, without moral guilt
H5355A.detail:
1. One who has not committed the evil of which he is suspected: this is innocence in a judicial sense, the purity of one who has not rendered himself guilty. When Rahab asks to be saved with her family (Joshua 2:19), she asks that the blood of the innocent not fall upon her — that is, those who do not participate in the rebellion not be punished.
2. One who is exonerated from guilt and its consequences: this is being freed from the punishment one deserves. The oath that Abraham's servant refuses in Genesis 24:41 would relieve him of responsibility if he failed — he would be innocent of having broken a promise that could not be demanded.
3. One who is free from a legal obligation or commitment: the word designates one who is not bound to do something. Thus, in Deuteronomy 24:5, a young married man is exempt from military service — he is freed from this obligation.
4. One whose blood has not been shed: this is the innocent in the specific sense of the law of blood. When Deuteronomy 19:13 speaks of removing innocent blood, it concerns punishing murder without just cause, protecting one who did not deserve to die.
5. One who is pure and blameless before God: moral and spiritual innocence, the absence of inner guilt. Psalm 24:4 describes one who ascends the hill of the Lord as having clean hands and a pure heart.
H5355A.origine: The Hebrew word נָקִי comes from a root that expresses the idea of being free, unburdened, exempt — like something that is not loaded. In the Old Testament, this same concept of purity and freedom from guilt appears in words of the same family. The basic image is of someone who is not chained by guilt or obligation: he breathes freely, he is not weighed down.
H5355A.emploi: This word appears about 40 times in the Old Testament, especially in legislative accounts and psalms. In Exodus and Deuteronomy, it describes one who should not be held responsible for an evil: the man whose ox kills someone unintentionally may be innocent of intentional murder (Exodus 21:28). In historical accounts (Joshua, Samuel, Kings), it qualifies blood shed without cause — this is the category of crime that cries out for vengeance (2 Kings 24:4). In the psalms and Job, it expresses the moral and spiritual purity that the believer asks of God (Psalm 24:4: clean hands, pure heart). In Isaiah and Jeremiah, the prophets denounce those who shed innocent blood, a serious violation of justice and covenant.
H5355A.portee: Understanding this word helps the Christian grasp what it means to be innocent before God. Innocence is not just the absence of guilt, but the purity of heart and justice towards others — especially the respect for human life. Through Christ's death, the believer is declared innocent before God (justified), freed from the guilt of his sin. But the word also reminds us that we are called to live innocently in our relationships with others, particularly by refusing violence and slander.

sens: who has not committed the crime or fault of which he is accused
who has not shed blood, exempt from murderous guilt
one who does not deserve the punishment he suffers
H5355B.detail:
1. The word describes a person who has done nothing wrong, who does not bear the guilt of an accusation: it is the absence of blame or responsibility in a wrongful action. In Joel 3:19, the children of Judah are called "innocent" because the Edomites killed them without them having committed any crime against them.
2. The word particularly applies to one who has not shed blood, who therefore does not bear the guilt of murder. In Jonah 1:14, the sailors plead with the Lord: "Do not charge us with innocent blood!" — they fear that the death of Jonah, who has done nothing wrong, will bring upon them the guilt of murder.
3. More broadly, it is one who suffers without deserving his suffering, whether it be death, punishment, or misfortune — the just who becomes a victim of injustice.
H5355B.origine: This word is a spelling variant of a Hebrew adjective meaning literally "pure" or "exempt from guilt." Its root refers to the idea of cleanness, moral purity: the one who is innocent is like "free from stain" on a moral level. The word belongs to the family of terms that express justice and innocence in the moral thought of the Old Testament.
H5355B.emploi: This word appears twice in the provided biblical Hebrew text. In Joel 3:19, it qualifies the blood of the children of Judah killed by Edom without reason, emphasizing the injustice of the crime. In Jonah 1:14, the sailors fear being responsible for the innocent blood of Jonah if they throw him into the sea. In both cases, it concerns blood shed — that is, murder — and the adjective emphasizes that the victim has done nothing to deserve death. The biblical context attaches great importance to the guilt of the one who sheds this blood: killing an innocent person is a grave sin that brings God's judgment.
H5355B.portee: The word "innocent" reminds the biblical reader that God protects and avenges those who suffer without deserving it. It calls for justice: one who kills the innocent incurs divine condemnation. It is also an invitation to moral honesty: not to charge innocent blood upon oneself is to refuse to participate in injustice and to respect the life that God has entrusted.

sens: State of being free from guilt or fault
Absence of punishment or condemnation
Purity of hands and heart in actions and intentions
H5356A.detail:
1. Innocence is primarily the absence of guilt — the fact of not having committed the fault one could be accused of. Abimelech can say in Genesis 20:5 that he acted "with a pure heart and innocent hands": he did not intentionally commit evil against Abraham. It is the state of one who has nothing to reproach themselves for.
2. Innocence also means escaping punishment or condemnation. To be innocent is not to deserve the punishment for what one is accused of.
3. Washing one's hands in innocence (Psalms 26:6) is an act that symbolizes purity — the psalmist affirms his moral integrity by accompanying this declaration with a concrete act. It shows through actions and heart that one lives according to righteousness. In Hosea 8:5, to purify oneself means to turn away from idolatry to regain lost innocence.
H5356A.origine: The word comes from the root niqua (נקה), which means "to be pure, to be white, to be innocent." The same root gives verbs that mean "to clean" or "to acquit." The basic image is that of physical purity — what is white and clean — but the word also applies to moral purity and the absence of guilt. This is why "innocent hands" evoke both concrete purity and life integrity.
H5356A.emploi: This word appears four times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and the narratives of Genesis. In the Psalms, innocence is a theme of prayer: the righteous affirms his innocence before God to obtain His protection or support (Psalms 26:6 and 73:13). In Genesis 20:5, it serves to justify prior conduct. In Hosea 8:5, the word relates to ritual or moral purification in the face of religious unfaithfulness. The usage shows that innocence is never just abstract: it is expressed through concrete acts and gestures.
H5356A.portee: For the believer, innocence reminds us of the importance of moral integrity and a good conscience. Washing one's hands in innocence is to invoke God while testifying to one's honesty and respect for His Law. This word also invites repentance: only the purification of the heart makes us truly innocent, not just the formal absence of guilt. It is an invitation to live in accordance with the righteousness that God expects from those who seek Him.

sens: Total lack of food in a region
Period when the land no longer produces crops
State of extreme deprivation and collective hunger
H5356B.detail:
1. The word denotes the complete absence of food, a crisis where provisions are lacking in a city or an entire region. It is a situation of distress where people suffer from hunger — not simply scarcity, but radical lack. In Amos 4:6, God says: "I sent famine in all your cities," meaning He deprived Israel of crops and bread to call them to repentance.
2. The word can also evoke more broadly the natural or divine phenomenon: the moment when fields cease to produce, when granaries empty, creating a social and spiritual catastrophe. Famine is never just a matter of an empty stomach in the Bible — it is an act of God, a judgment or correction.
H5356B.origine: The Hebrew word qehayon comes from a root that evokes the idea of "sending" or "striking" (the idea of a drought "sent" from heaven). It belongs to the family of words that describe calamities that befall a people. The concept of famine in the Old Testament is always linked to divine will: it is not a mere climatic accident, but a consequence of sin or a means of God's correction.
H5356B.emploi: The word appears once in the Bible, in Amos 4:6, in a context of divine judgment. The prophet Amos lists the punishments that God has sent to Israel to bring them back to Him — famine is among these signs of warning. It is presented as a weapon of God to lead His people to repentance, alongside other plagues like drought or crop destruction. The usage is clear and direct: famine is not passively endured; it is "sent" by the Lord.
H5356B.portee: This passage reminds the reader that God uses material trials and deprivations to call His people back to Him. Famine is not a definitive curse, but an invitation — the text says, "Yet you did not return to me." It teaches us that the difficulties of life are never absurd or pre-punished: they can be divine calls to conversion and a restored relationship with God.

sens: Narrow and elongated opening in the rock
Natural refuge or hiding place carved in stone
H5357.detail:
1. A fente is an opening, a crevice that divides the rock in two. It is what one sees when a stone cracks, creating a cavity where something can sink or slip in. In Isaiah 7:19, flies come to rest in the fentes of the rocks, like insects hiding in the interstices of the stone.

2. This fente also becomes a place where one can conceal something, a natural and discreet refuge. In Jeremiah 13:4, the prophet hides a belt in the fente of a rock, just as one would slip an object into a crevice. In Jeremiah 16:16, hunted men hide in the fentes of the rocks, fleeing their enemies: the fente becomes an asylum, a shelter to take refuge in.
H5357.origine: The Hebrew word naqiq comes from a root evoking the action of splitting, tearing, or digging. It literally describes what is split or what opens in two. The same root produces other words related to separation and rupture. It is a very visual word: it paints the image of a divided stone, with its natural hollow.
H5357.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always to designate the fentes of rocks. Isaiah uses it to describe where flies settle on the day of judgment. Jeremiah uses it twice: first for the symbolic act of the prophet hiding the belt (the sign of impending unfaithfulness), then to paint the picture of fugitives who hide in the rocks when the Lord chases them. The word remains concrete, without variation in meaning: it is always a crevice in the stone, sometimes an accidental shelter, sometimes a symbol of weakness and despair.
H5357.portee: This fente reminds us that man often seeks to hide in critical moments — it is human, it is weak. But it also illustrates how God knows every refuge: nothing can truly escape His work. The psalmist invokes God as a rock and a refuge; here, the fente of the rock shows the contrast: natural fentes are illusory hiding places in the face of divine judgment.

sens: To do justice by punishing one who has committed an unjust or violent act
To take revenge: to punish oneself the one who has offended or hurt you
To chastise, to inflict punishment in retaliation
To exercise vengeance in a sustained manner, to harbor vindictive feelings
H5358.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to do justice in reaction to a wrong or violence: it is to intervene to punish an evil act and repair the offense. In Joshua 10:13, Israel takes vengeance on its enemies by defeating them militarily — this is an act of collective justice.
2. When the subject takes revenge himself, he takes his own cause in hand to punish the one who has offended him. David refuses to take revenge on Saul in 1 Samuel 24:13, saying: "the Lord will avenge me of you," acknowledging that vengeance belongs to God alone.
3. In some contexts, the word designates the punishment itself, the chastisement inflicted in return for an injustice. In Leviticus 26:25, God warns: "I will take vengeance on such a nation," meaning He will punish them.
4. To harbor vindictive feelings is to maintain a persistent grudge, to cultivate the desire to punish. Leviticus 19:18 explicitly forbids this: "You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge."
H5358.origine: The Hebrew verb נָקַם comes from a root that evokes the idea of "burning" or "reacting strongly." It expresses a strong, immediate, and often passionate reaction to an injustice. The word is used in the Old Testament to describe both human acts of vengeance and, more importantly, God's action in exercising divine justice. It is a key word for understanding how Israel conceived restorative justice.
H5358.emploi: The verb appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Kings), poetic (Psalms), and prophetic (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It primarily describes human acts of vengeance, often warrior-like: Samson in Judges 15:7 cries, "I will take revenge on you." But it also applies, and especially, to God: He avenges the shed blood (Numbers 31:2), punishes injustice (Jeremiah 5:9, 5:29), and takes vengeance on the enemies of Israel (Nahum 1:2). An important meaning emerges in ethical prohibitions: Leviticus 19:18 forbids God's people from taking vengeance, revealing a tension between the human right to vengeance and the call to entrust justice to God alone.
H5358.portee: This word confronts the believer with a permanent question: to whom does justice and vengeance belong? The Bible acknowledges that vengeance is a human need in the face of injustice, but it forbids it to God's people to encourage them to entrust to God alone the right to punish. This frees one from the destructive weight of grudges and the thirst for personal vengeance, while reminding that God never leaves injustice unpunished.

sens: action of punishing someone who has done harm
punishment inflicted on an enemy or adversary
chastisement that God exercises against His enemies
divine retribution, reward and punishment
H5359.detail:
1. Vengeance is primarily the act of punishing someone who has committed an injustice or offense. Samson, after suffering harm from the Philistines who gouged out his eyes, asks God to give him strength to "take vengeance on the Philistines for my two eyes" (Judges 16:28): it is about retaliating, returning evil for evil.

2. It is also the punishment itself, the chastisement inflicted in reaction to an offense. The Lord declares: "I will bring the sword upon you, which will avenge my covenant" (Leviticus 26:25) — vengeance here is the consequence, the weight of judgment that falls upon the unfaithful.

3. Vengeance takes on a broader meaning when it designates the punishment that God exercises against His adversaries and enemies. God says: "If I sharpen the lightning of my sword and my hand takes hold of justice, I will take vengeance on my adversaries" (Deuteronomy 32:41) — it is the exercise of divine power to restore justice.

4. Vengeance becomes a divine virtue, a manifestation of God's justice: "He puts on righteousness as a breastplate... He takes vengeance for clothing" (Isaiah 59:17). It expresses that God does not tolerate injustice unpunished and that He restores the moral order of the universe.
H5359.origine: The Hebrew word נָקָם (naqam) comes from a root that expresses the idea of "striking back" or "inflicting a counter-attack." Vengeance presupposes a prior action — a wrong, an offense — that provokes a punitive reaction. In biblical thought, vengeance is not necessarily low or shameful: it can be the just exercise of an authority (royal or divine) to punish evil. God Himself is presented as the one who avenges — who justly punishes those who transgress His law or harm His people.
H5359.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the legislative books (Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and prophetic (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Micah). In humans, vengeance is an act of legitimate defense or justice: Samson claims it for the wrongs he has suffered. But more often, it is God who "avenges" — who punishes the transgressors of His covenant (Leviticus 26:25), who chastises the enemies of the Jewish people (Deuteronomy 32:41-43), or who executes His eschatological justice against the wicked nations (Isaiah 34:8, 63:4). The context always shows a link between the offense committed and the vengeance inflicted: it is the divine response to injustice.
H5359.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is not indifferent to injustice and evil. Divine vengeance is not an irrational passion, but the expression of His justice and concern for moral order. It comforts those who suffer oppression: "Take courage, do not be afraid; here is your God, vengeance will come" (Isaiah 35:4). But it also warns: no one can transgress God's law with impunity. This word urges the Christian to leave vengeance to God Himself and to trust in His justice, rather than seeking to take justice into their own hands.

sens: The act of punishing someone who has caused harm or damage
The act of God judging and punishing His enemies and those who have offended His people
The just retribution that God exercises against evil and injustice
H5360.detail:
1. Vengeance is primarily a concrete act: punishing someone who has wronged you by returning the same blow or worse. It is a natural human reaction to offense — when someone has hurt or stolen from you, you want them to pay. In Numbers 31:2, Moses is commanded to "avenge" the children of Israel on the Midianites who have seduced them: this involves a military expedition, an armed response.
2. In the Bible, vengeance takes on a more serious and solemn meaning: it is the act by which God Himself punishes His enemies and defends His people. Psalm 79:10 asks God to "avenge" the blood of His servants shed by the nations; Jeremiah 46:10 speaks of a "day of vengeance" when the Lord avenges His enemies. This is no longer a quarrel between humans, but divine judgment striking evil.
3. At the heart of divine vengeance lies the idea of justice: God restores order and right by punishing the one who has committed injustice. Jeremiah 51:6 calls it the "time of vengeance for the Lord," where "He will repay each according to his deeds" — God pays everyone according to what they have done.
H5360.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to strike back," "to respond to an offense." It expresses the idea of proportionality: the reaction must correspond to the harm suffered. This verb has given rise to the noun "vengeance," which designates the action itself. In biblical Hebrew, this word fits into a broader semantic field that includes justice, judgment, and retribution — fundamental concepts of the relationship between God and the people.
H5360.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms and the Prophets. It is found in the form of the verb ("avenge") and the noun ("vengeance"). At the beginning of the book of Numbers, vengeance is presented as a military mission entrusted by God. In the Psalms, it becomes a supplication: the psalmist asks God to avenge the blood of the innocents shed by enemies or the wicked. The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel use it to describe the future judgment that God will execute against Babylon, against the nations that have oppressed Israel. The meaning thus varies: an act of war when the people are involved, a supplication for justice when the righteous suffer, and a declaration of divine judgment when God announces the downfall of His enemies.
H5360.portee: This word helps the Christian understand that God is not indifferent to evil and injustice: He judges, He responds, He defends His own. But it also invites one not to take justice into their own hands — vengeance belongs to God. For those who suffer from injustice, this word provides assurance that God sees and will act. For those who have offended, it serves as a warning: God settles accounts.

sens: To separate from someone, to break a relationship
To cease to love or desire
To withdraw, to move away
H5361.detail:
1. The verb describes a separation that occurs between two people: one cuts off the other, breaking the bond that united them. It is an action that goes beyond mere physical distance — it is a rupture of the heart and attachment. In Ezekiel 23:18, God says that His heart "has detached" from the unfaithful woman, marking the interruption of a relationship that love once supported.
2. The word expresses a change in feeling: one ceases to love, one ceases to desire. Affection withdraws, desire fades. When in Ezekiel 23:22 God "stirs up against her her lovers, those whose hearts have detached from her," He describes a woman who has herself broken her ties with those she loved, who no longer desires her.
3. The verb can also mean to move away or withdraw: to leave the active relationship, to cease being involved. In Ezekiel 23:28, God delivers the woman "into the hands of those whose hearts have detached from her," those she has abandoned and separated from.
H5361.origine: The Hebrew verb נָקַע comes from a root evoking the idea of rupture or separation. Its basic meaning is physical — to cut off, to wean — but in these three passages from Ezekiel, it applies to the heart to express an emotional and relational separation. The translation as "detachment" of the heart captures well the image of an internal cut.
H5361.emploi: The verb appears only three times in Ezekiel 23 (verses 18, 22, and 28), all in the prophetic discourse against Oholiba, which represents unfaithful Jerusalem. In each occurrence, the subject of detachment is the heart: the heart of God that has detached from her (v. 18), then the hearts of her lovers from whom she has detached herself (v. 22 and 28). The context is one of blatant unfaithfulness and a definitive rupture of relationship. The word emphasizes irreversibility: what has detached does not easily reattach.
H5361.portee: This word reminds us that love and desire are not guaranteed to be eternal — unfaithfulness and repeated rejection eventually wear down even the strongest feelings, including those of God towards His people. It calls us not to take love for granted and to measure the cost of a voluntary rupture. For the believer, it also warns: divine patience has limits, and the persistent abandonment of the one who loves us inevitably leads to separation.

sens: To strike violently, to remove by a blow
To destroy or knock down by striking
To overturn, to make fall
H5362A.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to strike with force or to deliver a violent blow capable of removing or detaching something. In Job 19:26, it describes how the skin of the body can be "destroyed" — it is the image of an affliction that removes, gnaws, or detaches from what it covered.
2. The word is used to describe the action of knocking down, destroying solid things by a repeated or violent blow. In Isaiah 10:34, the Mighty "overturns" the thickets of the forest with iron — an image of massive and irresistible destruction, where the trees fall under the blows.
3. In these two uses, the word always evokes a brutal and definitive action: what is struck is destroyed, knocked down, or transformed in an irreversible manner.
H5362A.origine: The Hebrew verb naqaph comes from a root meaning "to strike" or "to give a blow." The word conveys the image of a violent, sudden action that removes or destroys. The equivalent Aramaic neqash carries the same meaning of "to strike" or "to hit." This verb belongs to the family of Hebrew words expressing violence and destruction by striking.
H5362A.emploi: This rare verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible with the meaning of "to strike" or "to destroy." In Job 19:26, it describes the destruction of the skin of the body by disease or death — an image of decomposition. In Isaiah 10:34, it evokes the massive cutting down of the forests of Lebanon by a military power. In both cases, the word emphasizes the violent, irresistible, and complete nature of destruction.
H5362A.portee: This word reminds believers that destruction and death are realities that must be faced with confidence in God. In Job 19:26, despite the ravaging of the body, Job proclaims his certainty of seeing God — faith transcends physical annihilation. The word invites one not to fear earthly ruin, but to fix their gaze on resurrection and eternal life.

sens: To go around something or someone
To wrap, encircle, enclose
To circle around, to prowl near
To complete a circuit, to travel a circular path
To manufacture or shape something by rounding its edges
H5362B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to go around, to circumvent: the ark of the Lord "went around the city" (Joshua 6:11), completing a full circumnavigation. It is a movement that creates a closed loop around a central point.

2. To wrap means to surround on all sides, like a net that imprisons: Job says that God "wraps him in His net" (Job 19:6), creating a situation where one is surrounded on all sides. The horses of the king of Aram "surrounded the city" (2 Kings 6:14), encircling it to besiege it.

3. To prowl around evokes a persistent and threatening presence: dogs and evildoers "prowl around" the psalmist (Psalms 22:17), circling around him like predators. The verb here suggests a threat that turns and watches.

4. To go around an object means to complete a full circular path, to travel its perimeter entirely, like the twelve bronze oxen that make the "circuit of the sea" (2 Chronicles 4:3) each supporting a part of its edge.

5. To cut or round the edges involves giving a rounded shape to something by working on it: it is forbidden to "cut the corners" of one's hair (Leviticus 19:27), that is, to round or trim the temples in a certain way.
H5362B.origine: The Hebrew root נקף (naqaph) evokes the image of circular movement, a circumvention. It is related to other Hebrew forms expressing the idea of turning, circumventing, or forming a loop. The word can describe both the action of tracing a circle and that of prowling or shaping. The verbal family in Hebrew groups meanings converging towards the idea of circularity and enclosure.
H5362B.emploi: The verb נקף appears 17 times in the Old Testament, mainly in narrative and poetic books. In the narratives, it describes military or processional movements: the ark circles Jericho (Joshua 6:11), the troops surround a city (2 Kings 6:14). In wisdom literature, it expresses an enveloping threat: enemies "prowl around" the psalmist (Psalms 22:17); God can "wrap" someone in His action (Job 19:6). The word is also used for material details: the oxen that "go around" a bronze basin (2 Chronicles 4:3), or the prohibition of cutting one's hair "in round" (Leviticus 19:27). The context determines whether the encirclement is protective (the ark sanctifying Jericho), threatening (the enemies), or simply technical (an ornament).
H5362B.portee: This verb reminds us that we live in a world where powers and threats often "surround" us (as in the psalms of distress), but also that God can "wrap" us in His presence and action. The circular movement that this word evokes — returning to the starting point, completing a round — invites reflection on divine providence and judgment, which encircle human history and bring it back to its ends.

sens: To shake a tree to make the fruit fall
To strip or ravage by force
H5363.detail:
1. To shake means to vigorously agitate a tree — particularly the olive tree — to detach the fruit. It is a concrete agricultural gesture: one shakes the tree, and the olives fall. In Isaiah 17:6, the prophet describes what remains after the harvest: "like when one shakes the olive tree, two or three olives at the top of the bough," an image of the little that remains.

2. By extension, to shake refers to the action of stripping or ravaging a land, emptying it of its riches like one empties a tree of its fruits. In Isaiah 24:13, this verb evokes divine judgment that leaves the land impoverished: "it will be in the land... like when one shakes the olive tree," an image of desolation and loss.
H5363.origine: The Hebrew word noqeph comes from a root meaning to strike, hit, or knock against. The image is one of shock, of repeated blows: one strikes the tree so that it yields its fruits. This root evokes the idea of percussion, of a violent but useful gesture. The word belongs to the vocabulary of harvest and agricultural work.
H5363.emploi: Noqeph appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Isaiah (17:6 and 24:13), in passages of divine judgment. In both cases, it describes the act of shaking the olive tree: in 17:6, it is an image of sparseness, of the little that remains to Israel after punishment; in 24:13, it is a sign of universal desolation on the day of judgment. The context is always one of loss and reduction to nothingness.
H5363.portee: This image of the shaken fruit reminds us that God's judgment leaves little standing. It also invites the believer not to rely on their riches or their own strength, which can be taken away as quickly as the olives fall from the tree. It is a word that calls for repentance and hope in divine mercy beyond punishment.

sens: A twisted or knotted link used to tie, hold, or gird
A symbol of servitude and degradation
H5364.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a rope is a manufactured link, generally twisted or knotted, used to tie, hold, or gird. In Isaiah 3:24, the prophet lists the depredations that Jerusalem will suffer: instead of the elegant belt of prosperous days, it will be a rope — a less noble, coarser, less adorned link.
2. Figuratively, the rope evokes servitude and loss of dignity. In this prophetic passage, it symbolizes impoverishment and humiliation: comfort and adornment give way to deprivation. It is a trait of the misery of times of divine judgment.
H5364.origine: The Hebrew word niqpah comes from a root that evokes the idea of encircling or girding. It belongs to the family of terms designating what surrounds or holds. In ancient Hebrew, ropes were everyday objects, essential for tying, binding, and girding (like a belt). The Greek text of the Old Testament (Septuagint) often translated it with a term designating a link or a belt.
H5364.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 3:24. It is found in a prophetic oracle where Isaiah announces the reversal of living conditions for the people of Judah. The prophet systematically lists what will be taken away (perfume, elegant belt, silky hair, magnificent clothing) and what will replace it (infection, coarse rope, baldness, narrow sack). The rope thus represents a humble, even degrading object, in contrast to signs of wealth and respectability.
H5364.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage reminds us that divine judgment reverses the values of the world: wealth and adornment can be suddenly taken away. Beyond that, it invites us not to base our dignity on external appearances. At the same time, it shows that God had long ago announced the consequences of unfaithfulness, demonstrating His patience and seriousness toward His people.

sens: To make a hole, a cavity in a hard material by removing substance
To gouge, pierce, remove an organ or part of the body
To extract, draw something from its source or mass
To erode, wear away by digging
H5365.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of manual labor: to dig a pit, a well, to make an excavation. It is the action of removing material from depth to create a cavity — as one digs into rock or stone (Isaiah 51:1, where Israel was 'drawn' from the depths of the pit).

2. This verb is particularly used for gouging or removing the eyes, that is, tearing them out or piercing them. This is the torture inflicted on Samson by the Philistines: they 'gouged out his eyes' (Judges 16:21), or the threat from Nahash who proposes to gouge out the right eye of every Israelite (1 Samuel 11:2).

3. Broadly, the word can mean to extract or draw something from its original source. Israel was 'drawn' from the rock and the pit (Isaiah 51:1), in the sense that God extracted it from its original condition.

4. Finally, it can describe an action that gnaws or erodes: the pain 'tears' Job's bones (Job 30:17), as if it were digging into his body from the inside. The ravens 'will gouge out' the eye of the rebellious son (Proverbs 30:17), embedding it into the flesh.
H5365.origine: The Hebrew verb נָקַר comes from a root that expresses the idea of digging, piercing, forcibly removing. This root evokes the image of an incisive, penetrating action: removing material, piercing a barrier, tearing away what adheres. The Qal form describes the simple action (to dig), the Piel form intensifies the effect (to dig deeper, to gouge completely), and the Pual form marks the passive result (to be dug out, to be torn away).
H5365.emploi: The verb נָקַר appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and wisdom books. It primarily denotes violent acts: gouging out Samson's eyes or threatening to do so is a punishment from ancient Levantine wars. In Job and Proverbs, it appears in a figurative or physical sense to describe suffering (the pain that tears) or the fate of the wicked (the birds that gouge the corpse). Only once, in Isaiah 51:1, does it take on a theological hue: 'drawn from the pit' means that God has extracted Israel from slavery and oppression, as one draws a stone from its quarry. The context removes any violent character to express deliverance.
H5365.portee: This word first reminds us of the brutal reality of penal justice in antiquity: corporal punishments were merciless. It invites reflection on the gravity of rebellion and contempt for parental authority (Proverbs 30:17): the Bible does not hesitate to show the extreme consequences of sin. But in Isaiah 51:1, the same verb becomes a promise: God has 'drawn' you from the rock, extracted from nothing to make you His people. It is a word of hope addressed to discouraged Israelites, redirecting them to their divine origin and the creative power of God.

sens: Cavity or fissure in the rock
Dug or natural refuge in the stone
Protective shelter offered by God
H5366.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a cavity or crack in the rock, an opening in the stone. In Exodus 33:22, Moses must place himself in the 'cleft' of a rock to be protected when the glory of God passes by.
2. This cleft becomes a refuge, a place to hide. In Isaiah 2:21, the frightened inhabitants 'will enter the cracks of the rocks and the clefts of the stones' to escape the terror of the day of judgment.
3. The image gains spiritual richness: the cleft of the rock represents the safe shelter and intimacy with God, where He 'covers us with His hand' and protects us from His own fearsome majesty.
H5366.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning 'to dig' or 'to pierce'. It literally describes what is hollow, emptied, or holed. It is a concrete word that speaks of the empty space carved out in the rock, either naturally or through the wear of time.
H5366.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always referring to a rocky cavity that offers refuge. In Exodus 33:22, it is in the context of Moses' privilege: God personally offers him a cleft to protect him from an overwhelming manifestation of His glory. In Isaiah 2:21, it is in a context of eschatological dread: faced with divine judgment, humans take refuge in the cracks and clefts of the rocks, terrified. The word retains its literal meaning but carries an increasing significance: first simple protection, it becomes a symbol of the asylum that only the proximity of God can offer.
H5366.portee: This word teaches that God is a real, tangible refuge, capable of hiding and covering us. It also reminds us that the majesty of God is fearsome: even Moses, His friend, cannot bear it face to face. For the believer, the cleft of the rock evokes this universal need to rest in God, away from turmoil and fear.

sens: To strike, hit hard
To ensnare someone by catching them in a net or trap
To lay snares to harm
H5367.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning is to strike or bring down something with a blow — an action of brutal force.
2. The most frequent meaning in the Bible is to catch or confine someone in a trap, like a net or snare that captures them. Psalms 38:13 says: 'Those who seek my life set their traps' — the image is that of trap setters preparing secret snares. In Psalms 9:17, the Lord 'ensnares the wicked in the work of their own hands', meaning He captures them by the fruit of their own malice.
3. Figuratively, the trap becomes a ruse, a deception intended to harm or corrupt. In Deuteronomy 12:30, God warns Israel not to be 'caught in a trap' by imitating the religious practices of pagan nations — the danger is not a physical net, but the gradual seduction towards idolatry.
H5367.origine: The root יָקַשׁ evokes the image of catching, striking, or capturing. It relates to any form of capture or binding — hence the idea of a trap, knot, or snare that binds and holds. This verb belongs to the vocabulary of hunting and cunning.
H5367.emploi: The verb appears about 25 times in the Old Testament. In the Psalms (9:17, 38:13, 109:11), it describes the traps that the wicked set against the righteous or that God sets against evil. In 1 Samuel 28:9, a woman says to King Saul in disguise: 'Why do you set a trap for my life?' — threatening someone with a trap puts them in danger or betrays them. In Deuteronomy 12:30, the trap is spiritual: that of imitating idolatrous practices. The word can refer to the trap set (the action of the verb), the mechanism of the trap, or the capture itself.
H5367.portee: This word reminds us that evil often sets traps in secret, through cunning and snares rather than through open force. It warns us of moral vulnerability: one can be captured by gradual seduction, as Israel was on the brink of idolatry. It also assures us that God 'ensnares' the wicked — it is He who, ultimately, sets the trap and frees the captives.

sens: To hit or knock against each other
To clash (referring to knees trembling in fear)
To physically tremble due to intense emotion
H5368.detail: 1. The word denotes the action of striking or knocking: two objects hitting against each other. 2. In the only known biblical usage, it describes the knees of King Belshazzar knocking against each other (Daniel 5:6) — a vivid image of the physical terror that seizes him when he sees a supernatural hand writing on the wall of his palace. 3. This repeated knocking of the knees effectively expresses how fear manifests in the body: the legs become weak, the knees clash, and one can no longer stand upright.
H5368.origine: Aramaic word (the language of the text of Daniel 5) derived from the root נקף (naqaph), which means "to strike, to knock" or "to surround, to gird." This same root also appears in Hebrew (H5362: naqaph). The verb primarily expresses violent contact between two solid things.
H5368.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 5:6. The context is that of divine judgment manifested by a wondrous sign: Belshazzar, the king of Babylon, during a feast, sees a hand writing on the wall. This sudden vision inflicts extreme terror upon him, to the point that the knees that support him knock against each other — a vivid description of physical panic, the uncontrollable trembling that seizes the body when confronted with the impossible.
H5368.portee: This image of knees knocking together shows us that the fear of God (or confrontation with His power) first manifests in the body: it paralyzes, disarms, and removes all assurance. It is a lesson in humility for the reader: in the face of the reality of God, no human strength can stand.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
Father of Abner, uncle of King Saul
Son of Jehiel according to some genealogies
H5369G.detail:
1. Ner is a character from the Old Testament, a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time of King Saul. He is best known as the father of Abner, the powerful commander of Saul's army: "Abner, son of Ner, commander of his army" (1 Samuel 14:50).
2. Ner was the uncle of King Saul. He appears regularly in the accounts of the rivalry between Saul and David, particularly when his son Abner opposes David or joins him. David asserts his innocence of Abner's murder by saying: "I am forever innocent, before the Lord, of the blood of Abner, son of Ner" (2 Samuel 3:28).
3. According to some genealogical lists, Ner was the son of Jehiel and the father of Kish, which would make him the grandfather of King Saul, although this may be a confusion with a namesake.
H5369G.origine: The name Ner means "lamp" in Hebrew, evoking the light of an oil lamp. This figurative name suggests a function of illumination or guidance, perhaps given to an ancestor who had a leadership role. Ner belongs to an important family of Benjamin linked to the emerging royalty of Israel.
H5369G.emploi: Ner is mentioned 15 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of Samuel and Kings. He appears mainly as "father of Abner" in the accounts of the wars between the house of Saul and that of David (2 Samuel 2-3). His name is also cited in 1 Kings 2 when David enumerates the crimes of Joab, who killed Abner son of Ner. The genealogies in 1 Chronicles also mention him. His role in the biblical text remains secondary: he is mainly known through his son Abner, who plays a central role in the transition of power from Saul to David.
H5369G.portee: Ner reminds us that the great figures of the Bible are part of genealogies and families. The repeated mention of Abner "son of Ner" underscores the importance of familial loyalty and how the politics of ancient kingdoms were intertwined with kinship ties. His story also illustrates how power conflicts could cost the lives of even the greatest generals.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, father of Kish and grandfather of King Saul
H5369H.detail: Ner is a character from the Old Testament, a member of the tribe of Benjamin, who lived during the time of the united monarchy. He is best known as the father of Kish and grandfather of King Saul (1 Chronicles 8:33; 9:39). His name means "lamp" in Hebrew, but there is no particular connection between this meaning and his role in biblical history.
H5369H.origine: The name Ner (נֵר) literally means "lamp" or "light" in Hebrew. It is a simple noun, derived from the everyday vocabulary of daily life. The name was likely given to this ancestor of Saul in a common manner, without specific reference to his historical role. This same word appears elsewhere in the Bible to refer to physical lamps (as in the tabernacle).
H5369H.emploi: Ner appears twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages of 1 Chronicles (8:33 and 9:39) that list the same genealogy of the house of Saul. In these two verses, he is presented as the father of Kish, being part of the important genealogical lineage that leads to Saul's royalty. He represents an important generation in the dynastic history of Israel, although the Bible provides few details about his personal life or deeds.

sens: Major deity of the Assyrian-Babylonian pantheon
H5370.detail: Nergal is an important god in the religion of the Assyrians and Babylonians. His name means "hero" in Akkadian. In 2 Kings 17:30, we learn that the inhabitants of Kuth (a region of Babylon) worshiped Nergal among other idols they brought to Israel after the deportation of the northern kingdom.
H5370.origine: The word comes from the Akkadian name of this major deity of the Mesopotamian pantheon. Nergal was associated with plague, war, and the underworld in Babylonian mythology. His cult was particularly significant in Kuth, hence his connection with the deportees from that region settled in Israel.
H5370.emploi: Nergal appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 17:30. The context is that of the fall of the kingdom of Israel: after the Assyrian conquest, the inhabitants of the conquered territories are transferred to Israel and bring their gods with them. The text lists various foreign idols — Succoth-Benoth for the Babylonians, Nergal for the inhabitants of Kuth, Ashima for those of Hamath — showing how foreign idolatry was introduced into the land of Israel. It is a concrete example of the religious contamination that the Law feared.
H5370.portee: Nergal reminds the reader that Israel during the time of the kings was seduced by the false gods of neighboring nations. It serves as a warning about the dangers of religious assimilation and infidelity to the God of Israel. The worship of Nergal symbolizes the abandonment of the true God for dark powers.

sens: Babylonian military officer of King Nebuchadnezzar
Chief of the diviners or high-ranking magician
Commander of a unit in the conquering army
H5371G.detail:
1. Nergal-Scharetser is a Babylonian officer who appears in the account of the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BCE. His name literally means "prince of fire" in Babylonian. He is a historical figure confirmed by Assyrian and Babylonian documents of the time.

2. He holds an important religious and military function: he is presented as the "chief of the magicians," meaning he is responsible for the diviners and spiritual advisors of the king. In the ancient Near Eastern army, these experts played a decisive role in interpreting omens and guiding strategic decisions.

3. He is among the "chiefs of the king of Babylon" who enter Jerusalem after the victorious siege. He is not a mere soldier, but a significant commander, placed alongside other dignitaries of royal power.
H5371G.origine: The Babylonian name Nergal-sar-ezer is composed of two elements. Nergal is the name of the Babylonian god of war and plague. Sar means "prince" or "king," and ezer means "fire." The full name thus evokes "the prince of fire" or "the prince of the god Nergal." This type of theophoric name — a name containing the name of a deity — was common among high-ranking Babylonians, marking their affiliation with a patron god or their relationship to Babylonian divine power.
H5371G.emploi: Nergal-Scharetser appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Jeremiah 39:3. He is mentioned in the very specific context of the conquest of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar in 587 BCE. Several Babylonian military and administrative leaders are listed together, and Nergal-Scharetser holds a notable place among them. His title of "chief of the magicians" indicates that he combines military and religious responsibilities, which was typical of Babylonian elites. His unique biblical mention reflects the historical importance of this moment: the end of the kingdom of Judah and the beginning of the exile.
H5371G.portee: This name reminds the reader of the historical reality of Babylonian domination and the fulfillment of the prophecy of divine judgment on Jerusalem. The precise mention of these names of Assyrian officers reinforces the credibility of the account and shows that the prophets spoke of concrete historical events, not mere allegories.

sens: Babylonian official during the divided monarchy
chief diviner and commander in Nebuchadnezzar's army
H5371H.detail: Nergal-Sharezer is a high-ranking Babylonian official who appears during the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BCE. His name, which means "prince of fire," reflects Babylonian deities (Nergal was a god of fire and war). He holds an important position in the Babylonian king's army, serving both as chief diviner (one who consults omens) and as a military commander, which shows his influence with the king.
H5371H.origine: The name Nergal-Sharezer combines two Babylonian elements: Nergal, the name of a Babylonian deity associated with fire and war, and Sharezer, meaning "prince" or "chief." The structure of the name reveals how the Babylonians understood power: a delegation of divine powers. This type of composite name was common among high-ranking Babylonian dignitaries to express their status and religious function.
H5371H.emploi: Nergal-Sharezer appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 39:13, where he is mentioned among the princes of Babylon who gather after the fall of Jerusalem. The context shows that King Nebuchadnezzar sends him, along with other officials, to give orders concerning the prophet Jeremiah. This unique mention highlights his role as executor of royal decisions and a trusted person with the Babylonian sovereign.
H5371H.portee: Nergal-Sharezer illustrates how God uses pagan powers and their officials to accomplish His purposes. Even the high dignitaries of Babylon act according to God's will: here, unknowingly, they protect the prophet Jeremiah. This historical detail reminds us that God controls history and that no power, however great, escapes His sovereignty.

sens: Fragrant aromatic plant imported from India
Perfume or essence extracted from this plant
Object of luxury and wealth in love poems
H5373.detail:
1. Nard is a fragrant plant that grows in India and was brought to the Middle East as a precious exotic product. It is a real plant, with a strong pleasant scent. In Song of Solomon 1:12, the poet says that the nard "exhales its fragrance" while the king is present: the image is that of a substance that naturally spreads its scent around it.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the perfume or aromatic oil derived from this plant, which could have been used to anoint the body or clothing. Nard appears alongside other precious aromatics — saffron, cinnamon, myrrh, aloe — as a rare and costly substance.
3. In the poems of the Song of Solomon, nard symbolizes beauty, charm, and value: to say that something is like nard is to say that it is beautiful, delightful, and of great worth. Nard represents luxury accessible only to kings and beloved ones.
H5373.origine: The Hebrew word נֵרְדְּ comes from the Sanskrit "spikenard" or from Indian words designating this plant. It is a borrowing from distant Eastern languages, which shows that the Hebrews knew this plant through trade with India and far-off regions. The word has retained roughly the same form in several Semitic languages, always to designate the same exotic product.
H5373.emploi: The word "nard" appears only three times in the Bible, exclusively in the Song of Solomon, a collection of love poems. In chapter 1, verse 12, the beloved or the poet says that the nard exudes its fragrance: it is the image of a delightful scent that fills the air around the king. In verses 4:13-14, nard is listed among the most beautiful aromatics of a wonderful garden — saffron, cinnamon, myrrh, aloe — as one of the fragrant treasures that symbolize beauty and wealth. Nard is always linked to the idea of perfume, luxury, and sensual charm.
H5373.portee: Nard reminds us that in the Song of Solomon, love is also expressed through the senses — sight, smell, touch. This precious and distant plant suggests that true love deserves what is most beautiful and rare. For the Christian reader, nard may also evoke love for Jesus: to offer nard is to offer what is most precious, what costs, what fills the heart with a good fragrance.

sens: Man of Judah during the divided monarchy
H5374.detail: Neriah is the father of the prophet Baruch, the secretary and faithful companion of Jeremiah. He appears in the accounts of the prophet Jeremiah, particularly when the latter entrusts Baruch with the mission of writing down his words (Jeremiah 36:4) and reading them publicly in the temple. Neriah does not act directly in the biblical texts, but he is mentioned each time his son is referred to, which shows the importance of genealogy in Baruch's lineage.
H5374.origine: The name Neriah means "lamp (or light) of the Lord" in Hebrew, composed of נֵר ("lamp, light") and יָהּ ("Yah," an abbreviation of the divine name). This theophoric name (containing the name of God) expresses a trust in divine guidance. Neriah lived during the time of the divided kingdom of Judah, probably in the 7th century BCE.
H5374.emploi: Neriah is mentioned ten times in the book of Jeremiah, solely to identify Baruch as his son. He appears in three important contexts: during the renewal of the purchase contract for a field (Jeremiah 32:12 and 32:16), during the dictation of the prophetic words to Baruch who reads them in the temple (Jeremiah 36:4, 36:8, 36:14, 36:32), and in the last chapters of Jeremiah (43:3, 43:6, 45:1, 51:59). Although his personal role remains in the shadows, he is the father of a key figure in the transmission of God's Word to Israel.
H5374.portee: Neriah reminds us that God uses entire families to accomplish His work. His son Baruch, though less famous than the prophet Jeremiah, played a decisive role in writing down and preserving the words of the prophet, work without which we would not have the book of Jeremiah. This shows that faithfulness can be passed down from generation to generation and that discreet but constant roles are precious in God's eyes.

sens: To raise something from the ground or hold it up high
To transport something from one place to another
To remove or take something away
To speak, say, or express verbally
To exalt, glorify, or give importance to someone
To bear, endure, or suffer a burden
H5375G.detail:
1. Lifting something from the ground or holding it up high: this is primarily a simple physical gesture. God tells Hagar: "Lift up the boy" (Genesis 21:18), in other words: raise him from the ground and take him away. Abimelech "lifted" a branch from a tree (Judges 9:48) by raising it with an axe.
2. Transporting something from one place to another: one takes something and carries it elsewhere. Nehemiah "took" the wine and presented it to the king (Nehemiah 2:1): he carried it from the table to the king. The priests "lifted" the ark of the covenant (Joshua 3:6), meaning they raised it to carry it.
3. Removing or taking something away: the verb also means to withdraw, take away, or make disappear. A strong wind "took away" the locusts from Egypt (Exodus 10:19). It also refers to forgiving a sin, "lifting" it from before God.
4. To speak, say, or express verbally: figuratively, to "lift" a word means to pronounce it, to make it heard. Jeremiah is called to "utter" a lament over Tyre (Ezekiel 27:2). Women are called to "speak" a lament (Jeremiah 9:18).
5. To exalt, glorify, or give importance: a "lofty" cedar from Lebanon (Isaiah 2:13) is a tree that stands high in the sky. The Lord "lifts up" the oppressed, giving them dignity and honor.
6. To bear, endure, or suffer a burden: one "carries" a load, one endures it. This is also the meaning of the verb when God "bears" iniquity, meaning He imposes the weight of guilt.
H5375G.origine: The Hebrew verb נָשָׂא comes from a root that fundamentally means "to lift" or "to raise up." It primarily expresses a physical movement: one lifts something, one elevates it. This image of lifting naturally extends to other areas: carrying something, transporting, removing, and even speaking ("lifting the voice"). In biblical Hebrew, this verb is very frequent and its uses are very varied, reflecting this richness of images around the idea of "movement upwards" or "the action of taking charge."
H5375G.emploi: The verb נָשָׂא is extremely common in the Hebrew Bible (over 120 occurrences). It is first encountered in very concrete contexts: one lifts an object, one carries it, one takes it (Genesis 21:18, Judges 9:48, Nehemiah 2:1). It is also used in religious contexts: one lifts or takes offerings (2 Chronicles 24:11), one raises the ark (Joshua 3:6). In the Psalms and Isaiah, the verb takes on more figurative meanings: one "lifts" their eyes to the heavens (Psalms 121:1), one "exalts" the Lord by glorifying Him (Psalms 7:7). Prophecy often uses the verb to say that the prophet "utters" a word (Jeremiah 9:18, Ezekiel 27:2). The meaning thus enriches over the books, moving from physical gesture to moral and spiritual expression.
H5375G.portee: This verb helps us understand how the Bible speaks of the relationship with God: lifting one's eyes to Him (Psalms 121:1) is seeking His help. Lifting one's voice to speak is also lifting one's prayer to God. The verb reminds us that even simple gestures, like lifting or carrying something, express trust and obedience. Bearing a burden is also what Christ did for us: He bore our sins. Finally, "being lifted" or "being exalted" speaks of the glory and dignity that God gives to those who serve Him.

sens: To lift and transport something from one place to another
To support the weight of something, to hold it
To endure, bear a moral burden or load
To carry away, remove or take away
To rise, to be lifted up (in the passive)
To forgive, to remit a fault (figurative sense)
H5375H.detail:
1. To lift and transport: the most concrete meaning. Joshua 4:10 speaks of the priests who bore the ark in the Jordan; Genesis 37:25 recounts that the Midianites who took Joseph were "carrying him to Egypt."
2. To support the weight: to hold something in balance or on oneself without letting it fall. It is to bear a load with effort. Numbers 11:14: Moses says to God, "I cannot bear this people alone."
3. To endure a pain: a figurative sense where one "bears" guilt or a consequence. Genesis 4:13, Cain cries, "My punishment is more than I can bear," he cannot support its weight.
4. To remove, carry away: "to bear" in the sense of taking and carrying far away. Isaiah 57:13: "The wind will carry away all" the idols, will remove them.
5. To rise (passive): to be lifted up, to rise. Genesis 7:17: "The ark rose above the earth" (in the passive, it was lifted up by the waters).
6. To forgive: a very figurative sense where God "bears" or removes a fault, thus taking it away (Genesis 18:24-26 speaks of those who are borne back by destruction, but the underlying idea is that a fault "borne" is remitted).
H5375H.origine: Very ancient Hebrew root denoting the action of lifting and transporting. The same root gives rise to words related to lifting (nessi, the prince, one who is lifted up). The verb has several conjugations that nuance the meaning: the simple form (Qal) = to lift oneself; the passive form (Niphal) = to be lifted; the intensive form (Piel) = to bear continuously; the causative form (Hiphil) = to cause someone to bear. This richness of forms explains the diversity of biblical uses.
H5375H.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Bible (207 occurrences). It appears in all the books and covers very varied meanings depending on the context. In the Pentateuch (Genesis to Deuteronomy), it often describes the material bearing of the ark and cult objects (Exodus 25:14, Numbers 4:15). In historical narratives (Joshua, Judges, Samuel), it means to transport or support. In poetry and among the prophets, it takes on figurative meanings: to bear an emotional or moral burden (Genesis 4:13), implicitly to forgive a fault. The context thus determines whether we should translate as "to bear materially," "to support morally," or "to remove."
H5375H.portee: This rich word helps Christians understand that God is the one who "bears" our burdens and sins: He takes on their weight in our place. It also evokes our responsibility to bear one another in the community and to endure trials with faith. The notion of forgiveness linked to this verb reminds us that the sin "borne" by God is remitted, disappeared.

sens: Lift, carry, bear a weight or burden
Remove, take away, carry off
Bear the weight of an offense or guilt: not holding the offense against the one who committed it, letting it go
Exalt, elevate, honor
Desire, ardently aspire to something
H5375I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to lift or carry something heavy. It is the gesture of one who takes a burden on their shoulders to carry it away. For example, lifting someone off the ground, or carrying a child.

2. The verb also means "to remove," "to take away" — it is the action of carrying something off to make it disappear. When we say "remove sin," we make it disappear.

3. The most common meaning in the Bible is "to forgive": it is to bear the weight of an offense without holding it against the one who committed it. God "bears" the guilt, meaning He removes it from the account of the guilty. In Psalms 32:1, we read: "Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven" — literally "carried" away. In Numbers 14:19, we ask God to "forgive" the iniquity of the people: this is asking Him not to punish, to remove this fault from before Him.

4. The verb can also mean "to exalt" or "to elevate" someone in honor and dignity — it is to lift high, to give consideration.

5. Rarely, it means "to desire" or "to ardently aspire": it is like "lifting one's eyes" toward something one covets.
H5375I.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of lifting, raising up. The same verb produces the noun שְׂאֵת ("dignity, favor") and אָשָׁם ("guilt"). The basic image — lifting a weight, carrying it — naturally extends to forgiveness: God "lifts" or "bears" the sin of the one He forgives, instead of allowing it to weigh on the guilty. This is why forgiveness in Hebrew is thought of as an act of merciful justice: to remove, to carry away, to make disappear.
H5375I.emploi: This verb appears 23 times in the provided usages, especially in contexts of forgiveness and divine grace. In the historical books and the Psalms, it designates the act of forgiving a fault, a transgression, or an iniquity (Genesis 50:17, Numbers 14:19, Psalms 25:18). The subject is almost always God or a king: it is the authority to forgive, to bear sin. In Exodus 32:32 and 34:7, we see that forgiveness is an exceptional grace, linked to God's mercy. In Psalms 85:3 and 99:8, forgiveness is presented as a covering of sin — God "bears" the iniquity of the people by not punishing it. The verb also applies to God who "does not absolve the guilty" (Exodus 34:7): here, He does not bear, does not forgive. The constant idea is that of a power that removes, bears, and thereby forgives or retains.
H5375I.portee: This word reveals that biblical forgiveness is not a simple forgetting: it is an active and powerful act, where the one who forgives "bears" the weight of the offense. Only God, in His strength and mercy, can "lift" sin, that is, make it disappear. For the believer, understanding that God forgives by "bearing" the fault changes everything: it shows that forgiveness costs the one who gives it, that it is not free in a weak sense, but an act of powerful grace. In Jesus Christ, this reality becomes visible: He "bears" our sins to the cross (Isaiah 53).

sens: Lift, raise something from the ground
Support a weight, a burden
Endure a pain, suffer a consequence
Remove, take away, carry off
Support, tolerate someone or something
Forgive, erase a guilt
H5375J.detail:
1. To lift or raise: the most basic, physical meaning. One lifts their eyes, raises something up (Exodus 28:38, where Aaron bears on his forehead the plate that holds the iniquities).
2. To support a weight, a burden: to physically support, but also figuratively to bear a moral or material burden. It is the idea of the bearer who holds something in balance (2 Kings 18:14, where the king agrees to bear the imposed tax).
3. To endure a pain, to suffer the consequences: the guilty "bears" their guilt, meaning they suffer the weight and effects of it. This can mean death or deprivation (Numbers 14:34, where the Israelites will bear the penalty of their iniquity for forty years).
4. To remove, take away, carry off: the word describes the movement that separates something from a place or person and carries it elsewhere. The scapegoat carries the sins into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:22).
5. To support someone or a situation: to tolerate, endure without revolt or flight, to accept living with (Leviticus 19:17, where one must bear their neighbor).
6. To forgive, erase the guilt: when God "bears" sin, He removes it from the one who committed it, taking it upon Himself. It is the liberating action of forgiveness (Isaiah 53:12, where the Servant bears the sins of many).
H5375J.origine: The Hebrew root נשא fundamentally expresses the idea of lifting, raising up. It is very ancient and very common in all Semitic languages. The basic image — lifting a weight — naturally extends to the idea of bearing, enduring, and then bearing the responsibility for a fault. It is from this same root that the word for "burden" in Hebrew comes. The notion of "forgiveness" arises from the image of the priest who removes the weight of sin from the penitent to place it elsewhere, like the goat that carries the sins into the wilderness.
H5375J.emploi: This verb appears 36 times in the provided usages, especially in the Law (Leviticus and Numbers) and among the prophets (Ezekiel, Isaiah). It first designates the concrete act of bearing a physical load. But very quickly, especially in ritual and legal texts, the word shifts to a moral sense: "to bear" sin means to suffer the consequence of it, or (when it is God who bears) to forgive. Aaron bears the iniquities of Israel on his forehead plate (Exodus 28:38): he assumes responsibility before God. The scapegoat carries away the sins (Leviticus 16:22): it removes them from the community. Hezekiah agrees to bear the Assyrian tributes (2 Kings 18:14): he accepts the imposed burden. In Isaiah, the suffering Servant bears our diseases and our sins (Isaiah 53:12): it is the image of absolute forgiveness. The word thus oscillates between physical effort, legal responsibility, and love that takes upon itself.
H5375J.portee: This word opens the heart to the reality of sin and its consequences: sin has a weight, a gravity, something that must be "borne." But it also reveals the heart of God: when the Lord "bears" sin instead of punishing it, it is an act of absolute grace. For the believer, this means that guilt can be removed, transferred, forgiven — which Jesus accomplishes by bearing our sins on the cross. It is a word of liberation.

sens: To lift, raise something with effort
To bear, endure, tolerate a burden or difficult situation
To accept, forgive a fault or offense
To be worthy of, deserve (for a person)
To rise, grow in importance or power
H5375K.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to lift or raise something off the ground, to hoist it upward. It is the act of carrying something from one place to another, as one would lift a heavy object.

2. The word expands to the idea of bearing a burden — not only physical but also moral or psychological. In Deuteronomy 24:15, the poor "hastens" (lit. "his soul lifts toward") to receive his wages: he has an urgent need, a desire that lifts him up. Similarly, "to suffice" in Genesis 13:6 means that the land cannot "bear" or "support" the wealth and population of the two groups.

3. In the moral and judicial realm, to lift a fault means to forgive it, to remove it, to erase it — it is to take away the weight of sin. Here the word aligns with the idea of removing something from someone.

4. To lift someone also means to honor them, to raise them from humiliation, to give them prestige. In Ezra 8:36, the governors "honor" the people, meaning they lift them up, treat them with respect.

5. Figuratively, a person or a nation can rise, exalt: to move from a low position to one of strength or authority.
H5375K.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root evoking the act of lifting, raising upward — the primary image is that of upward movement. The verb has several grammatical forms that nuance the meaning: the simple form (Qal) means to lift oneself; the passive form (Niphal) means to be lifted, to rise; the intensive form (Piel) adds the idea of continuous help or support. This same root generates common expressions in Hebrew for actions as varied as to take, remove, forgive, or honor — all linked to this central idea of lifting or carrying.
H5375K.emploi: This verb is very frequent in biblical Hebrew, used about 650 times. It appears in the provided usages mainly in contexts of capacity (the land cannot "suffice"), urgency or desire (the soul "longs"), and honor or support ("to honor," "to lend"). Its meanings vary according to context: when it concerns land or a place that cannot "suffice" to accommodate people, it is the meaning of capacity to support; when it concerns a person in need or fear, it is urgency or desire that manifests; when it concerns human relationships (to honor, to lend), it is the idea of help and recognition. The verb thus adapts to each situation, always retaining the underlying image of lifting, supporting, or removing.
H5375K.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on how God "bears" His people — He supports, forgives, honors. Conversely, it reminds us of our personal inability to bear our burdens without help, and our need for forgiveness. It also shows that human weakness has dignity: God can lift up the one who has fallen, honor the one who is despised. It is a word of hope for those who bend under the weight.

sens: To physically lift something upward
To bear, support the weight of something
To take, remove, take away
To exalt someone in honor, rank, or power
To rise, stand up with pride
To forgive a fault, to take it away
H5375L.detail:
1. To lift upward: this is the concrete gesture of raising something from the ground or from where it is. It is the basic physical action.
2. To bear weight: this means to support, to hold a burden on oneself. The word describes one who carries a load and supports it — for example, carrying a child or enduring suffering.
3. To take and remove: this means to take something from one place to carry it away. In this sense, forgiveness occurs when one "takes away" guilt (God removes sin).
4. To exalt, give dignity: this means to elevate someone in honor and power. The Lord "exalts" David by making him king (2 Samuel 5:12); the king "exalts" Haman by placing him above other officials (Esther 5:11). It is to put someone in a position of strength and respect.
5. To stand up with arrogance: this means to raise oneself with pride, to elevate oneself in one's own eyes. Moses and Aaron are accused of "exalting" themselves above the assembly (Numbers 16:3) — they claim more than their share.
6. To forgive: to remove a sin, to carry it away. It is the idea that one takes away the weight of guilt.
H5375L.origine: This Hebrew root הנשא comes from a very simple image: that of lifting, raising. The primary meaning is physical and gestural. The word has extended to the moral and religious idea: to elevate someone is to grow them, honor them, raise them higher.
