The word recalls the very sound of difficult breathing — a rapid and noisy breath that comes from the mouth and nose. This root also evokes the idea of breathing, of living, since breath is life itself for the Hebrews.
H5395.emploi: This verb appears only once in the entire Bible, in Isaiah 42:14. God speaks of Himself in the image of a woman in labor: after a long silence, He will finally cry out, pant, and blow. The context shows that God is revealing His power and passion — His determination to act becomes almost carnal, human, visceral. It is a moment when God expresses intense emotion.
H5395.portee: This word reminds us that God is not distant: He can speak of Himself in terms of embodied passion, difficult breathing, emotion that shakes the body. This helps us understand that emotion is not contrary to divine dignity, but can express it. For us, to pant in prayer or supplication is a true gesture, expressing the intensity of our waiting and desire.

sens: The vital breath that animates the body and allows for breathing
Life itself, that which sustains a living being
What only God can control and take away
H5396.detail: 1. Breath literally refers to the vital breath, the air we breathe that fills the lungs — it is the most concrete sign of life. 2. By extension, it represents life itself, that which makes a being exist and act: "God holds your breath and all your ways in His hand" (Daniel 5:23) means that He controls your entire life, from the first breath to the last. 3. The word also emphasizes the fragility of life: it depends entirely on God, fragile as a breath that can disappear at any moment.
H5396.origine: This Aramaic word (nishma) comes from the same root as the Hebrew word neshama (נְשָׁמָה), which also means "breath" or "respiration." The root evokes the image of breath coming from the mouth, the warm and living breath. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word is mainly used to refer to the breath of life that God gives, or the spirit that animates a person.
H5396.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Daniel 5:23. It is a passage where the prophet denounces King Belshazzar: the king has rebelled against the God of heaven by profaning His sacred vessels, worshiping mute and powerless idols, while the true God holds his own breath — his life — in His hand. The usage emphasizes the contrast: human gods see nothing, hear nothing, know nothing, but the living God controls the breath of the one who rises against Him.
H5396.portee: This word reminds us of a fundamental truth for faith: our life is not our property, but a gift from God, as fragile and dependent as a breath. Only God holds our existence in His hands — our breathing, our days, our future. This should humble human pride and nurture gratitude and obedience.

sens: The vital breath that animates a living being, the physical breath of respiration
The breath of all living beings, everything that lives
The spirit or principle of life that God places in man
The breath of God, an expression of His power or anger
H5397.detail:
1. The word "breath" primarily refers to physical breath, the air that enters and exits the nostrils. In Genesis 2:7, God "breathed" into the nostrils of the man created from dust: this divine breath gave him life, and he became a living being. It is the very act of breathing, what is perceived, what animates the body.
2. From this comes the broader sense of respiration and life: "everything that breathes." In Joshua 10:40, when Joshua "struck down all the land," he "did not let anyone escape" and "devoted to destruction everything that breathed." The word then refers to living beings, all creatures that need to breathe to live.
3. Breath also becomes the seat of consciousness, the spirit or soul. In Job 33:4, "the Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life": here, breath is what gives not only bodily life but also intelligence and consciousness.
4. Finally, the text speaks of the breath of God as an expression of His fearsome power. In 2 Samuel 22:16, "the blast of the breath of His nostrils" uncovers the foundations of the world — it is the power of God that acts, threatens, and destroys.
H5397.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to breathe, to blow." It is from the same family as words relating to breath and wind. The image is always that of physical breath: what comes from the nostrils, what lives and moves. The central idea is that life is a breath, something subtle and invisible that depends entirely on God. In Hebrew, this word is close to "nephesh" (the soul, the living person), but with the emphasis on breath rather than the whole being.
H5397.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the Old Testament. It is mainly used in poetry and primordial narrative: Genesis (creation of man), Psalms, and Job. In history (Joshua, 1 Kings, 2 Samuel), it means "to breathe" or "that which breathes," speaking of the life of creatures and men. In poetry (Job, Psalms, Isaiah), it takes on a more spiritual meaning: breath becomes the expression of the divine spirit, or the principle of consciousness in man. In Job 4:9 and Job 34:14, the breath of God kills or gives life; in Isaiah 42:5, it is God who "gives breath" to all beings. The word always oscillates between the physical (breathing) and the spiritual (the spirit, the divine vital force).
H5397.portee: This word reminds us that life itself is a gift from God, something precious and fragile. Every breath is a creative act of God that keeps us alive. It also teaches us that our spiritual life, our consciousness, our spirit, depend entirely on God just like our physical breath. The breath of God is never far away: it creates, it animates, it can also judge. This should make us humble and grateful.

sens: To expel air from the mouth or nostrils with force
To annihilate or disperse something by this breath
To carry away quickly and completely
H5398.detail:
1. To blow is the physical action of expelling air forcefully: in Exodus 15:10, God blows with His breath, and this movement of air causes the Egyptians to sink in the sea like lead. It is a concrete and powerful act.
2. This breath can also destroy or make disappear: in Isaiah 40:24, God blows on the rootless plants and they wither immediately. The image evokes total fragility in the face of this force.
3. The meaning generalizes: to blow then means to make disappear, to annihilate, to carry everything away at once. Things that are blown away collapse like chaff in the wind, without resistance.
H5398.origine: The Hebrew word נָשַׁף comes from a root that expresses the idea of a violent breath, close to the word that designates wind or breath. This root always evokes a force that acts at a distance, without direct contact, by simple projection of air. It is the image of a power that does not touch but overturns.
H5398.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Bible. In Exodus 15:10, it is God who blows to engulf the Egyptian army in the Red Sea — an act of deliverance and judgment. In Isaiah 40:24, the same verb applies to the fragility of human powers before God: they are rootless and perish at the first divine breath. These two uses emphasize the power and sovereignty of God.
H5398.portee: This word reveals God's omnipotence: without effort, without weapon, a simple breath breaks what men thought was strong. For the believer, it reminds us that forces that seem invincible — injustice, oppression, false gods — are as fragile as chaff before God. It is a comforting assurance: what threatens will collapse at the moment chosen by Him who holds everything in His hands.

sens: Transition between night and day, at sunrise or sunset
Moment of relative darkness, conducive to hiding
State of confusion or uncertainty
Imminent end of a period
H5399.detail: 1. Twilight is that moment of the day when light fades at sunset or begins to dawn at dawn — those fleeting moments between full brightness and complete darkness. It is during these hours that the Syrians fled their camp in a panic (2 Kings 7:7), when the growing darkness made their escape difficult to discern. David pursued the enemy from dawn until twilight (1 Samuel 30:17), covering the entire bright day. 2. Twilight is also the hour when confusion and darkness reign, conducive to hidden acts — those who commit adultery wait for twilight to act without witnesses (Proverbs 7:9). 3. The word metaphorically evokes a state of discomfort or disorientation: to be in twilight is to grope like a blind person (Isaiah 59:10), not to see clearly. 4. It is also a near end, a decline: one who lives far from spiritual twilight (Jeremiah 13:16) still receives a chance to turn to God.
H5399.origine: The Hebrew word nevheph (נֶשֶׁף) comes from a root expressing the idea of breath or lightness, perhaps related to the flight of nocturnal creatures. It paints this moment of the day when light fades like a breath that extinguishes. It is a poetic term, more often used in wisdom and prophetic books than in historical narrative.
H5399.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetry and wisdom teaching. In historical texts (1 Samuel, 2 Kings), it designates precisely dawn or twilight as pivotal moments of the day. In wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Psalms), it takes on a moral or existential hue: twilight symbolizes the darkness of evil, the turmoil of the soul, or the inability to discern. In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah), it evokes decadence, spiritual blindness, or imminent judgment.
H5399.portee: Twilight reminds the reader that each day has its boundaries, each life its critical passages. It symbolizes the hours of uncertainty where one feels lost, but also of vigilance and calling: it is often at these pivotal moments that God acts. For the believer, meditating on twilight — whether at dawn or sunset — invites one to remain vigilant, to seek the light of the Lord when darkness threatens.
